lessons.title: Programming and the Structured Idea
lessons.content:
Imagine you have a robot friend who is super fast but knows absolutely nothing. It cannot guess, it cannot "kind of understand", and it never gets tired. If you tell it "make tea", it just stands there. But if you tell it "fill the kettle with water, switch it on, wait until it boils, put a tea bag in a cup, pour the water, wait two minutes, remove the bag, add sugar", it will make perfect tea every single time. That robot is a computer, and that list of exact steps is a program. This whole course is about learning to write those steps clearly, in a language called C.

What is a program: A program is a set of instructions written in a language the computer can follow, so that it does some job for us. A calculator app, the bKash app on your phone, the software that prints your bus ticket, and the game you play on your break are all programs. Each one is just a long list of small, precise steps. The computer does not understand meaning; it only follows the steps exactly. If a step is wrong, it will do the wrong thing very fast and very confidently.

What is an algorithm: Before we write a program, we usually think of an algorithm. An algorithm is a step-by-step method for solving a problem, written in plain language or in a simple form called pseudocode. It must be clear (no confusing steps), finite (it must stop at some point), and it must produce an answer. For example, an algorithm to find the bigger of two numbers A and B is: Step 1, read A and B. Step 2, if A is greater than B, the answer is A. Step 3, otherwise the answer is B. Step 4, print the answer and stop. A program is simply an algorithm written in a real programming language.

Flowcharts and pseudocode: Two popular ways to write an algorithm are flowcharts and pseudocode. A flowchart is a drawing: an oval for start and stop, a parallelogram for input and output, a rectangle for a processing step, and a diamond for a yes/no decision, all joined by arrows. Pseudocode is fake code: plain words arranged like a program, such as "IF A > B THEN print A ELSE print B". Neither runs on a computer, but both help you think clearly before you type.

From problem to program: Programmers usually follow a small routine. First, understand the problem: what goes in (input) and what should come out (output). Second, design an algorithm, maybe with a flowchart or pseudocode. Third, write the code. Fourth, compile and run it. Fifth, test it with different inputs, including tricky ones, and fix the mistakes, which we call bugs. Sixth, keep it tidy and add notes so others can understand it. Beginners often jump straight to step three and then get stuck. Spending five minutes on paper first saves an hour of confusion later.

What "structured" means: In the early days of programming, people wrote code that jumped all over the place using an instruction called goto, which means "jump to that line now". A program could jump forward, backward, into the middle of something, and out again. Such code was nicknamed spaghetti code, because following its path was like following one noodle in a plate of spaghetti. It worked, but nobody could read it, fix it or change it safely. Structured programming was the cure.

The big idea: Structured programming says that any program can be built using only three kinds of building blocks, each with one entry and one exit. In 1966, two computer scientists, Corrado Böhm and Giuseppe Jacopini, showed that these three blocks are enough to express any computation. In 1968, Edsger Dijkstra wrote a famous letter called "Go To Statement Considered Harmful", arguing that programmers should stop jumping around with goto. Together these ideas changed how the world writes code.

Sequence: The first building block is sequence: do steps one after another, from top to bottom. For example: read the price, read the quantity, multiply them, print the total. Nothing fancy happens; each line runs once, in order. Most of every program is plain sequence. In C, each of these steps is a statement ending with a semicolon, like total = price * quantity;.

Selection: The second block is selection, which means choosing between paths based on a condition. In everyday language: if it is raining, take an umbrella, otherwise wear sunglasses. In C it looks like if (marks >= 40) printf("Pass"); else printf("Fail");. Only one of the two paths runs. Selection lets programs make decisions, like a shop app giving a discount only if your bill is above 1000 taka.

Iteration: The third block is iteration, also called repetition or looping: repeat some steps while a condition is true. If you want to print the numbers 1 to 100, you do not write 100 print lines. You write a loop: start at 1, print the number, add 1, and repeat while the number is not more than 100. In C: for (i = 1; i <= 100; i++) printf("%d ", i);. Loops are where computers really shine, because they repeat millions of times without getting bored.

Putting the blocks together: These three blocks can be placed one after another or nested inside each other, like Lego pieces. A loop can contain an if, and an if can contain a loop. A program that prints only the even numbers from 1 to 20 is a loop (iteration) with an if inside it (selection), and inside the if there is a print step (sequence). Because each block has one way in and one way out, you can read the program from top to bottom and always know where you are.

Top-down design: Structured programming also means breaking a big problem into smaller problems, then breaking those into even smaller ones, until each piece is easy. This is called top-down design or stepwise refinement. Suppose the job is "make a result sheet for a class". You break it into: read student marks, calculate total and grade for each student, and print the sheet. Then "calculate grade" breaks into: if total is 80 or more give A+, else if 70 or more give A, and so on. In C, each piece usually becomes a function, which you will learn in detail later.

Why structured code is better: Structured programs are easier to read, because the flow goes top to bottom. They are easier to test, because you can check each small piece alone. They are easier to fix and change, because a change in one piece does not secretly break a far-away piece. And teams can work together, with each person writing different functions. That is why almost every modern language, from C to Python to Java, is built around these ideas.

A short history of C: C was created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in the USA in the early 1970s, around 1972. It grew out of an earlier language called B, written by Ken Thompson. Ritchie and Thompson used C to rewrite the Unix operating system, which was a big deal, because before that operating systems were mostly written in assembly language, which is tied to one kind of machine. In 1978, Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie published the book "The C Programming Language", which programmers still call K&R. Later C was standardized: ANSI C in 1989 (often called C89), then C99, C11, C17 and the newer C23.

Why learn C first: C is small, fast and close to the hardware. It shows you how memory really works, with addresses and bytes, instead of hiding it. Linux, parts of Windows and macOS, the firmware in washing machines and microwaves, and many embedded devices are written in C or C++. Languages like C++, Java, C#, JavaScript and Go borrow C's style of braces, semicolons and operators, so once you know C, you can read many other languages. Most Bangladeshi universities teach C as the first programming course for exactly these reasons.

C is a procedural language: In C, you organize your program as a set of procedures, called functions, that work on data. You tell the computer how to do something step by step. This is different from object-oriented languages like Java, where you organize code around objects. Do not worry about that difference now; you will meet object-oriented programming in a later course. For now, think of C as a toolbox of steps and functions.

Compiled, not interpreted: C is a compiled language. You write the source code in a file, for example hello.c, and a program called a compiler translates the whole file into machine code that the processor can run directly. This is why C programs are very fast. Python, by contrast, is usually run by an interpreter that reads and runs your code piece by piece. We will see how to compile and run your first program in the next lesson.

Real life example 1, the tea stall: Think of a tea stall near your university gate. The tea seller follows a structured routine. Sequence: take a cup, add milk, add tea liquor. Selection: if the customer says "chini kom", add less sugar, otherwise add the normal amount. Iteration: while there are customers in the line, keep making tea. And top-down design: the owner splits the job, one boy washes cups, one takes money, one makes tea. Each person is like a function doing one job. No goto, no chaos, and the line moves fast.

Real life example 2, the exam result: Think of how your SSC or HSC result is processed. For every student (iteration), the system reads marks for each subject (sequence), calculates the grade point for each subject using rules like "if marks are 80 or more, grade point is 5" (selection), and then computes the GPA. The whole job is broken into smaller jobs: reading data, grading, calculating GPA, and publishing. Each one is a separate piece that can be tested alone. This is structured programming at a national scale.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Many students think structured programming means "programming with structures (struct)". It does not; struct is a separate C feature. Structured programming is about clean control flow using sequence, selection and iteration. Another confusion is algorithm versus program: the algorithm is the idea and steps, the program is that idea written in a specific language. Typical exam questions include: define structured programming and list its three control structures; why is goto discouraged; what is top-down design; who developed C and when; and write an algorithm or flowchart for a small problem such as finding the largest of three numbers.

Recap: A program is a precise list of instructions, and an algorithm is the plan behind it. Structured programming builds every program from three blocks, sequence, selection and iteration, and avoids messy goto jumps. Big problems are broken down top-down into small pieces. C, created by Dennis Ritchie around 1972, is the classic language for learning this style, because it is simple, fast and close to the machine. In the next lesson you will write, compile and run your very first C program.
key_points: A program is a precise list of instructions; an algorithm is the step-by-step plan behind it.
Structured programming uses only three control structures: sequence, selection and iteration.
Each structure has one entry and one exit, so code reads top to bottom.
goto jumps create hard-to-read 'spaghetti code'; Dijkstra argued against it in 1968.
Top-down design breaks a big problem into small pieces, usually functions in C.
C was created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs around 1972 and used to rewrite Unix.
C is a compiled, procedural language that is fast and close to the hardware.
lessons.tip: Before typing any code, write the steps on paper in plain words. If you cannot explain the steps to a friend, the computer will not understand them either.

quiz.q: Which three control structures are enough to build any structured program?
quiz.explain: Böhm and Jacopini showed that sequence, selection and iteration are enough to express any computation.

options: It makes programs slower to compile
It is not allowed in C
It makes the flow jump around and code hard to read and fix
quiz.explain: goto exists in C, but jumping around creates 'spaghetti code' that is hard to follow, test and change.

quiz.explain: Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs in the early 1970s.

quiz.explain: Choosing a path based on a condition is selection.

quiz.explain: Top-down design (stepwise refinement) splits a big task into smaller, easier tasks.

lessons.title: Your First C Program
lessons.content:
Remember the first time you rode a bicycle? Someone held the seat, you wobbled, and after a few metres you were moving on your own. Your first C program is that first ride. It is tiny, it does almost nothing, but once it runs on your own computer, you have crossed the biggest wall in programming. In this lesson we write that program, look at every line, and see what happens between typing the code and seeing the output.

The classic first program: For more than 40 years, almost every C learner has started with a program that prints "Hello, World!". Here it is, line by line. Line 1: #include <stdio.h>. Line 2: int main(void) {. Line 3: printf("Hello, World!\n");. Line 4: return 0;. Line 5: }. When you run it, the screen shows Hello, World! and the program ends. Five lines, but each one teaches something important.

#include <stdio.h>: Lines starting with # are instructions for the preprocessor, a helper that runs before the real compiling starts. #include tells it: copy the contents of this header file here. stdio.h stands for standard input output header. It contains the declarations of functions like printf and scanf. Without it, the compiler would not know what printf is supposed to look like. Think of it as telling the chef which spice box to bring to the kitchen before cooking starts.

The main function: int main(void) is where every C program starts running. No matter how many functions your program has, the computer always begins at main. The word int before main says that main gives back an integer to the operating system when it finishes. void inside the brackets says main takes no input here. You will also see int main() written with empty brackets, which is common in textbooks. The curly braces { and } mark the start and end of main's body, the block of statements that belong to it.

printf and statements: printf("Hello, World!\n"); is a statement that calls the printf function to print text. The text inside double quotes is called a string literal. The \n at the end is an escape sequence meaning "newline", so the cursor moves to the next line after printing. Every statement in C ends with a semicolon. The semicolon is like a full stop at the end of a sentence; forgetting it is the most common error beginners make.

return 0: return 0; ends main and sends the value 0 back to the operating system. By tradition, 0 means "everything went fine", and a non-zero value means something went wrong. In modern C, if main reaches its closing brace without a return, it behaves as if it returned 0, but writing it clearly is a good habit and many teachers expect it in exams.

The general structure: A typical C program has a few sections in this order. First, documentation comments describing what the program does and who wrote it. Second, preprocessor lines like #include and #define. Third, global declarations, such as variables or function prototypes used everywhere. Fourth, the main function. Fifth, other user-defined functions. Small programs only need the #include and main, but this layout is what exam questions mean when they ask you to "describe the structure of a C program".

Source code to running program: The file you type, for example hello.c, is the source code. It is just text; the processor cannot run it directly. To turn it into a program, it goes through four stages. Preprocessing handles the # lines, pasting in headers and replacing macros. Compiling translates the C code into assembly or machine instructions and checks the grammar. Assembling turns assembly into an object file, often named hello.o, which contains machine code. Linking joins your object file with library code, such as the real code of printf, to produce the final executable file.

Seeing the stages yourself: gcc lets you stop after each stage, which is a great way to understand them. gcc -E hello.c shows the code after preprocessing; you will be surprised that your five lines became hundreds, because stdio.h was pasted in. gcc -S hello.c stops after compiling and writes hello.s, an assembly file you can open and read. gcc -c hello.c stops after assembling and writes the object file hello.o. Finally gcc hello.o -o hello does only the linking. You do not need these every day, but trying them once makes the four stages real instead of just words in a textbook.

Using gcc: The most common free C compiler is GCC, the GNU Compiler Collection. On Linux or macOS you open a terminal and type gcc hello.c -o hello. This does all four stages and creates an executable called hello. Then you run it with ./hello. On Windows, people often install a package called MinGW which provides gcc, and the output file becomes hello.exe. The -o option simply names the output file; without it, gcc uses a default name such as a.out on Linux.

The executable belongs to its machine: The executable file that gcc produces contains machine code for one kind of processor and one operating system. A hello.exe built on Windows will not run on a Mac, and a program built for an Intel or AMD laptop will not run directly on an ARM-based phone. The C source code, however, is portable: you can take hello.c to another computer and compile it there. That idea, write once in C, compile anywhere, is one of the reasons C spread so fast in the 1970s and 1980s.

IDEs: Typing commands is fine, but many beginners use an IDE, an Integrated Development Environment. An IDE gives you an editor, a compiler and a debugger in one window, with a big Build and Run button. In Bangladeshi universities you will often see Code::Blocks, and some people use Dev-C++, Visual Studio Code with a C extension, or online compilers that run in a browser. Behind the button, the IDE is usually calling a compiler such as gcc for you. Learn at least the gcc command once, so the button is not magic.

Printing more than text: printf can print numbers too, using placeholders called format specifiers. printf("Age: %d\n", 20); prints Age: 20, because %d is replaced by the integer after the comma. printf("%d + %d = %d\n", 2, 3, 2 + 3); prints 2 + 3 = 5. You will study printf and scanf properly in lesson 5, but it is fun to try a few now. Change the numbers, run again, and watch the output change. Every time you edit the source, you must compile again, because the old executable still contains the old code.

Syntax errors: When you make a grammar mistake, the compiler refuses to build the program and prints an error with a line number. Forgetting a semicolon, missing a closing brace, writing Printf with a capital P, or misspelling a variable name are syntax or compile errors. Read the first error message carefully, fix it, and compile again. Often one small mistake causes a long list of errors, and fixing the first one makes the rest disappear.

Linker errors: Sometimes the code compiles but linking fails. For example, if you call a function named calcTotal but never write it, the compiler may accept the call but the linker complains "undefined reference to calcTotal". If you misspell main as mian, the linker cannot find the starting point and also reports an undefined reference. Linker errors mean "I could not find the code for something you used".

Runtime errors: A program can compile and link perfectly and still crash while running. Dividing an integer by zero, reading memory you do not own, or running out of memory are runtime errors. The program may stop suddenly with a message like "Segmentation fault" or "Floating point exception". These are harder to find, because the compiler cannot always see them in advance.

Logical errors: The sneakiest errors are logical errors. The program runs and prints an answer, but the answer is wrong. For example, if you write average = a + b / 2; you get a plus half of b, not the average, because division happens before addition. The fix is average = (a + b) / 2;. The compiler cannot catch logical errors, because the code is perfectly legal C. Only testing with known answers catches them.

Warnings: Besides errors, compilers print warnings: things that are legal but suspicious, like using a variable before giving it a value. A warning still lets the program build, but you should treat warnings as friendly alarms. Compile with gcc -Wall hello.c -o hello to turn on most common warnings. Good programmers keep their code warning-free.

Comments and layout: You can write notes for humans inside the code. A comment starting with // runs to the end of the line, and a comment between /* and */ can cover many lines. The compiler ignores comments. C also ignores extra spaces and blank lines, so you could write the whole program on one line, but nobody could read it. Indent the body of main by four spaces, and put one statement on each line.

A good working routine: Make a separate folder for this course, for example cprog, and save each program with a clear name like 01_hello.c or 02_sum.c. Edit, save, compile, run, and repeat in small steps. Add one or two lines at a time and compile often, instead of writing fifty lines and then facing fifty errors. Keep a notebook page called "errors I met" and write each new error message and its fix. After a few weeks you will recognise most messages instantly, which is exactly how experienced programmers look so calm in front of red error text.

Real life example 1, the cyber cafe printout: Think of sending a document to a print shop in Nilkhet. You write the text (source code). The shop owner checks it for missing pages (compiling). He adds a cover page and a binding from his stock (linking with libraries). Then he prints the final copy (the executable) and hands it to you to use (running). If you forgot a page, he refuses to print (syntax error). If the cover belongs to someone else, it is a mix-up at the binding stage (linker error). And if the content itself is wrong, he prints it happily, because he only checks the format (logical error).

Real life example 2, the mobile recharge message: A shop's recharge machine prints "Recharge successful" after each top-up. Inside, a tiny C-like program does printf("Recharge of %d taka successful\n", amount); and returns 0 to say all is well. If the network fails, the program returns a non-zero code, and the shop's system knows to show "Try again". That return value is the same idea as return 0 in your first program.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Common beginner errors are a missing semicolon, writing Main instead of main (C is case-sensitive), forgetting #include <stdio.h>, using single quotes for strings ('Hello' instead of "Hello"), and saving the file as .txt instead of .c. Exams often ask: describe the basic structure of a C program; what is the role of the preprocessor, compiler and linker; differentiate syntax, runtime and logical errors with examples; what does return 0 mean; and what is the purpose of #include <stdio.h>.

Recap: Your first program has a preprocessor line, the main function, a printf statement and return 0. Source code goes through preprocessing, compiling, assembling and linking to become an executable. gcc hello.c -o hello builds it, and ./hello runs it. Errors come in four flavours: syntax, linker, runtime and logical, and the last is the hardest to spot. In the next lesson we look at the small pieces C code is made of: tokens, keywords, identifiers, variables and constants.
key_points: Every C program starts running from main().
#include <stdio.h> brings in declarations for printf and scanf.
Every statement ends with a semicolon; C is case-sensitive.
Build stages: preprocessing, compiling, assembling, linking.
gcc hello.c -o hello builds; ./hello runs the program.
return 0 tells the operating system the program finished successfully.
Error types: syntax (compile), linker, runtime and logical.
lessons.tip: Type every program yourself instead of copy-pasting. Your fingers learn the semicolons and braces, and you will make (and fix) the common mistakes early.
lessons.task: Write and run Hello World, then break it on purpose: remove a semicolon, change main to mian, and remove the #include line. Note the exact message the compiler gives each time.

quiz.q: Where does every C program start executing?
options: At the first line of the file
quiz.explain: Execution always begins at main(), no matter where it is written in the file.

quiz.q: Which stage joins your code with the real code of library functions like printf?
quiz.explain: The linker combines object files with library code to make the executable.

quiz.q: A program runs but prints a wrong average. This is a:
quiz.explain: The code is legal and runs, but the logic is wrong, so it is a logical error.

quiz.q: What does return 0; in main usually mean?
quiz.explain: By convention 0 tells the operating system the program finished without problems.

quiz.q: What does \n inside printf do?
options: Moves the output to a new line
quiz.explain: \n is the newline escape sequence.

lessons.title: Tokens, Variables and Constants
lessons.content:
Think about how you learned Bangla or English as a small child. First letters, then words, then sentences, and only then stories. C works the same way. Before writing big programs, you need to know its alphabet, its words and the rules for naming things. This lesson is the "letters and words" lesson of C: character set, tokens, keywords, identifiers, variables, constants and comments. It looks simple, but almost every compile error a beginner meets comes from breaking one of these small rules.

The character set: C programs are written using a fixed set of characters. These are the uppercase letters A to Z, the lowercase letters a to z, the digits 0 to 9, special symbols such as + - * / % = < > ( ) { } [ ] ; , . ' " # & | ! ? : ^ ~ _ and the backslash, and white space such as spaces, tabs and newlines. You can write Bangla text inside a string or a comment on most modern systems, but the code itself, the names and keywords, must use this basic set.

Tokens: When the compiler reads your program, it first chops the text into the smallest meaningful pieces, called tokens, just as you split a sentence into words. In the statement int total = price * 2; the tokens are int, total, =, price, *, 2 and ;. C has six kinds of tokens: keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and special symbols (also called punctuators, like braces, brackets, commas and semicolons). Spaces separate tokens but are not tokens themselves, which is why int total and int     total mean exactly the same thing.

Keywords: Keywords are words that C has reserved for its own use, each with a fixed meaning. You cannot use them as names for your variables. The original ANSI C standard (C89) has 32 keywords: auto, break, case, char, const, continue, default, do, double, else, enum, extern, float, for, goto, if, int, long, register, return, short, signed, sizeof, static, struct, switch, typedef, union, unsigned, void, volatile and while. Later standards added a few more, such as inline and _Bool in C99. All keywords are written in lowercase, so int is a keyword but INT is not.

Identifiers: An identifier is a name you invent for something: a variable, a function, an array, a structure. total, studentAge, find_max and main are identifiers. Good names make code read like a story. Compare int a, b, c; with int price, quantity, total;. Both work, but the second tells you what is happening without any comment. In large programs, choosing good names is one of the most important habits you can build.

Rules for identifiers: C has strict naming rules. First, a name may contain only letters, digits and the underscore. Second, it must not start with a digit, so 2ndScore is illegal but score2 is fine. Third, it cannot be a keyword, so you cannot name a variable int or while. Fourth, no spaces or other symbols: student age and total$ are illegal, but student_age is fine. Fifth, C is case-sensitive, so Total, total and TOTAL are three different names. Names beginning with an underscore followed by a capital letter are reserved for the system, so avoid starting names with an underscore.

Valid or not, a quick quiz: Let us check a few. roll_no is valid. _count is allowed but better avoided. 9lives is invalid because it starts with a digit. my-name is invalid because the minus sign is an operator, so C would read it as my minus name. float is invalid because it is a keyword, but Float or float1 are valid (though confusing). totalMarks2024 is valid. In exams you often get a list like this and must mark each as valid or invalid with a reason.

Naming styles: Two popular styles are snake_case, like total_marks, and camelCase, like totalMarks. C programmers traditionally prefer snake_case, and constants are often written in ALL_CAPS, like MAX_SIZE. Whichever you choose, be consistent in one program. Short names like i, j and n are fine for loop counters, but use clear names for anything that carries meaning.

Variables: A variable is a named memory location that holds a value which can change while the program runs. Imagine a row of labelled jars in your mother's kitchen: one says "salt", one says "sugar". The label is the variable name, the jar is the memory location, and what is inside is the value. You can refill a jar with a different amount later, just as you can store a new value in a variable.

Declaring a variable: In C you must declare a variable before you use it, telling the compiler its type and its name. int age; declares an integer variable named age. float price; declares a variable for decimal numbers. You can declare several at once: int a, b, c;. Declaration makes the compiler reserve the right amount of memory for that type. Using a name that was never declared is a compile error: "undeclared identifier".

Initializing a variable: Giving a variable its first value is called initialization. You can do it in the declaration, int age = 20;, or later with an assignment, age = 20;. Here is an important warning: a local variable inside a function that is declared but not initialized does not automatically become 0. Its value is indeterminate, often called a garbage value, whatever bits were left in that memory. If you write int sum; and then sum = sum + 5;, the result is unpredictable. Always initialize counters and totals, for example int sum = 0;.

Assignment is not equality: The = sign in C means "put the value on the right into the variable on the left". So x = x + 1; is perfectly sensible in C: take the current x, add 1, and store it back in x. In mathematics x = x + 1 is impossible, but in C it simply means "increase x by one". The left side of an assignment must be something that can hold a value, such as a variable. Writing 5 = x; is an error, because you cannot store anything into the number 5.

Constants: A constant is a value that does not change while the program runs. When you write 25, 3.14 or 'A' directly in code, these are literal constants. Integer constants can be written in decimal like 25, in octal with a leading zero like 031 (which is 25 in decimal), or in hexadecimal with 0x like 0x19 (also 25). Be careful: writing 010 in C does not mean ten; it means octal 10, which is eight. Floating-point constants have a decimal point or an exponent, like 3.14 or 2.5e3, which means 2.5 times 10 to the power 3, so 2500.0.

Character and string constants: A character constant is a single character inside single quotes, like 'A', '7' or '$'. Internally it is stored as a small number, its character code; in ASCII, 'A' is 65 and '0' is 48. A string constant is a sequence of characters inside double quotes, like "Dhaka". Do not mix them up: 'A' is one character, while "A" is a string of two characters, the letter A followed by a hidden end marker. You will study strings in detail in lesson 18.

Named constants with const: Sometimes a value should never change, like the number of days in a week. You can say const int DAYS = 7;. Now if any line tries DAYS = 8;, the compiler stops you with an error. This protects you from accidental changes and makes the meaning clear: anyone reading DAYS knows exactly what 7 stands for.

Symbolic constants with #define: Another common way is the preprocessor: #define PI 3.1416. Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces every PI in your code with 3.1416. There is no semicolon at the end of a #define line, and no = sign. The difference from const is that #define is pure text replacement with no type, while a const variable has a type the compiler can check. Both are used widely; lesson 24 covers #define in more depth.

Escape sequences: Some characters are hard to type inside quotes, so C uses escape sequences starting with a backslash. \n is newline, \t is a tab, \\ is a backslash itself, \" is a double quote inside a string, \' is a single quote, and \0 is the null character, which marks the end of a string. So printf("He said \"Hi\"\n"); prints He said "Hi" and then moves to a new line.

Comments: Comments are notes for humans that the compiler ignores. A single-line comment starts with // and runs to the end of the line, for example int age = 20; // student's age. A multi-line comment starts with /* and ends with */. Multi-line comments cannot be nested: putting /* inside another /* ... */ comment ends the comment early at the first */. Write comments that explain why you did something, not what each obvious line does. "x = x + 1; // add one to x" adds nothing, but "// skip the header row" helps.

Real life example 1, the class register: Think of the attendance register in your school. Each student has a roll number, which must be unique and follow a rule, like an identifier. The headings at the top, like "Name", "Roll", "Present", are fixed by the school and you cannot use them as student names, just like keywords. Each day's tick or cross can change, like a variable's value, but the number of working days fixed for the year is like a constant. And the small notes in the margin, "absent due to fever", are comments: useful to people, ignored by the counting.

Real life example 2, a bKash style balance: Imagine a tiny program for a mobile wallet. const int MAX_SEND = 25000; could store a fixed daily limit (a made-up number for this example). int balance = 5000; is a variable, because the balance changes with every transaction. When you send 500 taka, the program does balance = balance - 500;. If the programmer forgot to initialize balance, the starting value would be garbage and users might see a random number. This is why careful declaration and initialization really matter in money-related software.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Typical mistakes are starting a name with a digit, using a keyword as a name, using a hyphen instead of an underscore, forgetting that C is case-sensitive (declaring Total and then using total), forgetting to initialize sums, putting a semicolon at the end of #define, and writing 010 expecting ten. Exams commonly ask: what is a token and what are its types; list some keywords; state the rules for identifiers and mark a list as valid or invalid; differentiate variable and constant; differentiate const and #define; and what is an escape sequence.

Recap: C code is built from tokens: keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and special symbols. Keywords are reserved lowercase words. Identifiers are your own names and must follow the rules: letters, digits and underscore, not starting with a digit, no keywords, case-sensitive. Variables are named memory boxes that must be declared, and should be initialized. Constants never change and can be literals, const variables or #define symbols. Comments are for humans. In the next lesson we look closely at data types, the "kind" of each box, and how much memory each one uses.
key_points: The compiler splits code into tokens: keywords, identifiers, constants, strings, operators, special symbols.
C89 has 32 lowercase keywords such as int, if, while and return; they cannot be used as names.
Identifiers use letters, digits and underscore, cannot start with a digit, and are case-sensitive.
A variable is a named memory location; declare it with a type before use.
Uninitialized local variables hold garbage values; initialize sums and counters.
Constants: literals (25, 3.14, 'A', "Hi"), const variables, and #define symbols.
A leading 0 means octal (010 is eight) and 0x means hexadecimal.
Comments (// and /* */) are ignored by the compiler and should explain why.
lessons.tip: Make a pocket list of the 32 keywords and read it aloud once a day for a week. Most identifier questions in exams become free marks.
lessons.task: Mark each name as valid or invalid with a reason: total_marks, 2ndRoll, my-name, _temp, while, While, price$, roll123. Then declare three variables of your own with good names and initial values.

quiz.explain: student_age uses only letters and underscore and does not start with a digit.

quiz.q: What is the value of an uninitialized local int variable?
quiz.explain: Local variables are not set to zero automatically; their value is indeterminate.

quiz.q: What decimal value does the C constant 010 have?
quiz.explain: A leading zero means octal, and octal 10 equals 8 in decimal.

options: It is replaced by the preprocessor before compiling
It needs a semicolon at the end
It can be changed later with PI = 3;

quiz.explain: The tokens are int, x, =, 5 and ; which makes five.

lessons.title: Data Types and Memory Sizes
lessons.content:
Walk into a kitchen and look at the containers. A tiny bowl for salt, a jar for sugar, a big drum for rice, a bottle for oil. You would never pour oil into the salt bowl or store a sack of rice in a teacup. Each container is the right size and shape for what it holds. Data types in C are exactly that: they decide what kind of value a variable can hold, how much memory it gets, and what you can do with it. Choosing the right type is one of the first real decisions a C programmer makes.

Why types matter: Inside the computer, everything is stored as bits, zeros and ones, grouped into bytes of 8 bits. The same bit pattern can mean a whole number, a decimal number or a letter, depending on how you read it. The data type tells the compiler how many bytes to reserve and how to interpret those bits. It also decides which operations make sense. Dividing two integers gives an integer, while dividing two decimals gives a decimal, so the type even changes the answer.

The basic types: C has a small set of basic (primary) data types. char holds a single character or a small integer. int holds whole numbers. float holds numbers with a fractional part, with single precision. double holds numbers with a fractional part, with double precision, meaning more digits of accuracy. There is also void, which means "no value" and is used, for example, for functions that return nothing. On top of these, C builds derived types like arrays, pointers, structures and unions, which you will meet in later lessons.

int: int is the everyday type for whole numbers: roll numbers, counts, ages, marks. The C standard only promises that an int is at least 16 bits, but on almost all modern computers an int is 4 bytes, which is 32 bits. A 4-byte int can hold values from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647, roughly minus two billion to plus two billion. Example: int students = 120; int temperature = -5;. If you try to store 3.7 in an int, the fractional part is simply dropped and you get 3.

char: char is the smallest type, exactly 1 byte. It stores one character, like char grade = 'A';. Behind the scenes, the character is stored as its code number. In ASCII, 'A' is 65, 'B' is 66, 'a' is 97 and '0' is 48. That is why you can do arithmetic with characters: 'A' + 1 gives 66, which is 'B'. A signed char usually holds -128 to 127 and an unsigned char holds 0 to 255. Whether a plain char is signed or unsigned depends on the compiler, which is a classic tricky detail.

float and double: For prices, averages, heights and CGPAs you need decimals. float usually takes 4 bytes and gives about 6 to 7 significant decimal digits of precision. double usually takes 8 bytes and gives about 15 to 16 significant digits. Example: float cgpa = 3.75; double pi = 3.141592653589793;. In C, a decimal constant like 3.75 is a double by default; to write a float constant you add f, as in 3.75f. Most programmers use double unless memory is very tight, because the extra precision avoids many small errors.

Floating-point is not exact: Computers store float and double in binary, and many simple decimals, like 0.1, cannot be stored exactly in binary, just as 1/3 cannot be written exactly in decimal (0.3333...). So 0.1 + 0.2 might be stored as 0.30000000000000004 instead of exactly 0.3. This is why you should not compare floating numbers with == for exact equality. Instead, check whether the difference is very small, for example if the absolute difference is less than 0.000001. For money, programs often count in poisha as integers to avoid this problem.

Type modifiers: C lets you adjust the basic types with modifiers: short, long, signed and unsigned. short int (or just short) is usually 2 bytes, holding -32,768 to 32,767. long int is at least 4 bytes; on 64-bit Linux and macOS it is usually 8 bytes, while on Windows it is usually 4. long long int, added in C99, is at least 8 bytes and can hold numbers up to about 9.2 quintillion (9.2 × 10^18). long double is a float type with at least the precision of double, often more.

signed and unsigned: By default, int is signed, meaning it can hold negative and positive values. unsigned int gives up negative numbers and uses all its bits for positive values, so a 4-byte unsigned int holds 0 to 4,294,967,295. Use unsigned when a value can never be negative and you need the extra range, like counting bytes. But be careful: mixing signed and unsigned values in comparisons can give surprising results, because the signed value may be converted to a huge unsigned number.

The sizeof operator: You do not have to memorize sizes for every computer, because C has the sizeof operator. sizeof(int) tells you how many bytes an int uses on this machine. printf("%zu\n", sizeof(int)); might print 4. sizeof(char) is always 1 by definition. You can also apply sizeof to a variable, like sizeof(price). %zu is the format specifier for the size type that sizeof returns; on older compilers you may see %lu or %d with a cast instead.

A typical size table: On a common 64-bit Linux computer with gcc, you will usually see: char 1 byte, short 2 bytes, int 4 bytes, long 8 bytes, long long 8 bytes, float 4 bytes, double 8 bytes, and long double 16 bytes. On 64-bit Windows, long is 4 bytes instead. This difference is exactly why exams sometimes say "assume int is 4 bytes" and why careful programmers use sizeof instead of guessing.

How ranges are calculated: The range comes from the number of bits. With n bits, an unsigned type can hold 2^n different values, from 0 to 2^n - 1. For 8 bits, that is 0 to 255. A signed type usually uses two's complement, which splits the range: from -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1. For 8 bits that gives -128 to 127; for 16 bits, -32,768 to 32,767; for 32 bits, about -2.1 billion to 2.1 billion. You learned two's complement in the computer systems course, and here it becomes real.

limits.h and float.h: C provides headers that tell you the exact limits on your system. limits.h defines constants like INT_MAX, INT_MIN, CHAR_MAX and UINT_MAX. float.h defines FLT_MAX, DBL_MAX and the precision constants. printf("%d\n", INT_MAX); on a typical computer prints 2147483647. Using these names is better than typing big numbers by hand.

Overflow: What happens if a value goes beyond the range? For unsigned types, the result wraps around like a car odometer: if an unsigned char holds 255 and you add 1, it becomes 0. For signed types, overflow is undefined behavior in C, which means the standard does not say what happens; on many machines it wraps to a negative number, but you must never rely on that. A real example: int big = 2147483647; big = big + 1; is a bug. If you expect large values, use long long.

Choosing the right type: Use int for normal counts and whole numbers. Use long long when numbers can exceed about two billion, such as the population of a country multiplied by something, or a factorial bigger than 12! (because 13! is 6,227,020,800, which does not fit in a 4-byte int). Use double for measurements, averages and scientific values. Use char for single characters. Use unsigned only when you have a clear reason. Picking types carefully prevents silent bugs.

A worked mini program: Let us put types together. Suppose we want the area of a circular pond with radius 7 metres. We write: double radius = 7.0; double area = 3.14159 * radius * radius; printf("Area = %f\n", area);. The output is about 153.938. Now try the same with int radius = 7; int area = 3.14159 * radius * radius;. The calculation is done in double, giving 153.938, but storing it in int area cuts it down to 153. Nothing crashed, no error appeared, yet you lost information. This is the quiet danger of a wrong type, and why the type should match the meaning of the value, not just whatever is quickest to type.

Booleans: C did not originally have a true/false type. Any non-zero value counts as true and zero counts as false. C99 added _Bool and the header stdbool.h, which gives you bool, true and false, so you can write bool passed = true;. Under the hood, true is 1 and false is 0. Many older textbooks simply use int with 1 and 0.

Real life example 1, a shop's inventory: Imagine writing software for a grocery shop in your area. The number of eggs in stock is an int, because you cannot have half an egg on the shelf. The price of 1 kg of rice, like 72.50 taka, is a double. The product category code, like 'V' for vegetables, is a char. The total sales of a big supermarket chain in a year could exceed two billion poisha, so it should be a long long. Each choice comes from asking: what kind of value is this, how big can it get, and does it need decimals?

Real life example 2, the cricket scoreboard: In a cricket app, runs and wickets are ints. The run rate, like 6.45 runs per over, is a double. The batting team's first letter on a small display could be a char. The total number of balls bowled in all international matches ever would be a very large count, so long long is safer. And whether the match is live could be a bool. A good programmer looks at the data first and picks the type that fits, just like picking the right container in the kitchen.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Common mistakes include storing a decimal in an int and losing the fraction, comparing floats with ==, assuming int is always 2 bytes (it was on old 16-bit Turbo C, which some books still use) or always 4 bytes, ignoring overflow when multiplying big numbers, and forgetting that 'A' and "A" are different. Exams ask: list the basic data types with their sizes and ranges; what are type modifiers; difference between float and double; what is sizeof; calculate the range of an n-bit signed or unsigned integer; and what is overflow.

Recap: Data types decide how much memory a variable gets and how its bits are read. The basic types are char, int, float, double and void. Modifiers short, long, signed and unsigned change size and range. Sizes depend on the machine, so use sizeof and limits.h instead of guessing. Floating-point numbers are approximate, and integer overflow is a real bug. In the next lesson you will learn to talk to the user with printf and scanf, using the right format specifier for each type.
key_points: A data type sets how many bytes a variable uses and how its bits are interpreted.
Basic types: char (1 byte), int (usually 4), float (usually 4), double (usually 8), void.
Modifiers short, long, long long, signed and unsigned change size and range.
A 4-byte int holds about -2.1 billion to 2.1 billion; unsigned int holds 0 to about 4.29 billion.
Use sizeof and limits.h instead of guessing sizes; they differ between systems.
Floating-point values are approximate; do not compare them with == for exact equality.
Unsigned overflow wraps around; signed overflow is undefined behavior.
lessons.tip: Run a small program on your own computer that prints sizeof for every type. Keep the output in your notes; it is your machine's personal size table.
lessons.task: Write down the best type for each value with a reason: number of students in a class, CGPA, first letter of a name, population of Bangladesh, price of a book in taka and poisha, 20 factorial.

quiz.q: How many bytes does a char always take in C?
quiz.explain: sizeof(char) is 1 by definition in the C standard.

quiz.q: What happens with int x = 3.9; ?
quiz.explain: Converting a floating value to int drops the fractional part, so x is 3.

quiz.q: What is the range of an 8-bit unsigned integer?
quiz.explain: With 8 bits there are 256 values, from 0 to 2^8 - 1 = 255.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid comparing two doubles with ==?
options: Many decimals are stored approximately, so tiny errors appear
quiz.explain: Values like 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary, so results may differ slightly.

quiz.q: Which type is safest for 13 factorial (6,227,020,800)?
quiz.explain: It exceeds a 4-byte int's maximum of about 2.1 billion, so long long (at least 8 bytes) is needed.

lessons.title: Input and Output with printf and scanf
lessons.content:
A program that cannot talk is like a shopkeeper who never speaks and never listens. You walk in, ask for a kilo of potatoes, and he just stares. Not very useful. Programs become useful when they take information from us and show results back. In C, the two main tools for this are printf, which shows output, and scanf, which reads input. Both live in stdio.h. In this lesson you will learn how they work, how to format numbers neatly, and the small traps that catch almost every beginner.

Input and output in general: Input means data coming into the program: numbers typed on the keyboard, text from a file, readings from a sensor. Output means data going out: text on the screen, a file being written, a printed receipt. C does not have special keywords for input and output; instead, everything is done through library functions. By default, the keyboard is called standard input (stdin) and the screen is called standard output (stdout). The functions in this lesson use those two.

printf basics: printf stands for "print formatted". Its first argument is a format string in double quotes. Ordinary characters in it are printed as they are. Special placeholders starting with %, called format specifiers, are replaced by the values that follow. Example: int age = 19; printf("I am %d years old\n", age); prints I am 19 years old. You can print several values: printf("%d + %d = %d\n", 4, 5, 4 + 5); prints 4 + 5 = 9. The values are matched to the specifiers left to right, so the order matters.

The main format specifiers: %d (or %i) prints an int in decimal. %u prints an unsigned int. %ld prints a long and %lld a long long. %f prints a float or double in normal decimal form, with 6 digits after the point by default. %e prints in scientific form, like 1.234500e+03. %c prints a single character. %s prints a string. %x prints an integer in hexadecimal and %o in octal. %p prints a pointer address. And %% prints a percent sign itself, so printf("Discount: 10%%\n"); prints Discount: 10%.

Matching type and specifier: The specifier must match the type of the value. If you print a double with %d, or an int with %f, you do not get a nice conversion; you get a wrong, strange number, because printf reads the bits as the wrong type. This is undefined behavior. Many compilers warn you about such mismatches if you turn on warnings with -Wall, which is another good reason to keep warnings on.

Field width: You can control how wide a printed value is. %5d prints an integer in a field 5 characters wide, right-aligned, padding with spaces on the left. So printf("[%5d]", 42); prints [   42]. A minus sign makes it left-aligned: %-5d gives [42   ]. A zero pads with zeros: %05d gives [00042], which is handy for roll numbers or times like 09:05. If the number is wider than the field, it is printed in full; the width is a minimum, not a maximum.

Precision: For floating values, a dot and a number set how many digits appear after the decimal point. %.2f prints two digits after the point, rounding the value: printf("%.2f", 3.14159); prints 3.14, and printf("%.1f", 2.75); prints 2.8 (rounding at the exact middle can depend on the binary value, so do not rely on it in money code). You can combine width and precision: %8.2f prints the number with 2 decimals in a field 8 characters wide. This is how receipts and result sheets line up their columns neatly.

Printing a neat table: Suppose you want a small price list. printf("%-10s %8s\n", "Item", "Price"); then printf("%-10s %8.2f\n", "Rice", 72.5); then printf("%-10s %8.2f\n", "Lentils", 110.0);. The names are left-aligned in a 10-character column, and the prices are right-aligned with two decimals in an 8-character column. The result looks like a tidy table instead of a messy line of text.

What printf returns: printf is a function, and it returns the number of characters it printed. Most programs ignore this, but it is a common viva question. For example, int n = printf("Hello\n"); stores 6 in n, because Hello is five characters plus the newline.

scanf basics: scanf reads formatted input from the keyboard. It uses similar format specifiers, but you must give it the address of the variable where the value should go, using the & operator. int age; scanf("%d", &age); waits for the user to type a number and press Enter, then stores it in age. The & means "address of". scanf needs the address because it must change the variable, and in C a function can only change your variable if it knows where the variable lives in memory. You will understand this deeply in the pointers lessons.

Always prompt first: scanf waits silently. If your program calls scanf without printing anything first, the user sees a blinking cursor and has no idea what to type. So always print a clear prompt before reading, like printf("Enter your age: "); scanf("%d", &age);. Notice the prompt has no \n, so the cursor stays on the same line, which feels natural. On some systems the prompt might not appear before scanf waits, because output is also buffered; adding fflush(stdout); after the prompt forces it to appear. In most simple programs it shows up fine, but now you know the fix if it does not.

Reading several values: scanf("%d %d", &a, &b); reads two integers. The user can separate them with spaces, tabs or newlines, because %d skips leading white space automatically. For a float use %f, and for a double use %lf. This is a key difference from printf: in printf, %f works for both float and double, but in scanf, %f is for float and %lf is for double. Mixing them up gives wrong values.

What scanf returns: scanf returns the number of values it successfully read and stored. If you call scanf("%d", &x); and the user types abc, scanf returns 0, and x is not changed. Careful programs check this: if (scanf("%d", &x) != 1) { printf("Invalid input\n"); }. It is a simple habit that makes your programs much more robust.

The %c trap: Reading a character after a number is a famous problem. If you do scanf("%d", &n); and then scanf("%c", &ch);, the second scanf often reads the leftover newline from when the user pressed Enter, so ch becomes '\n' and the program seems to skip the input. The fix is to put a space before %c: scanf(" %c", &ch);. The space tells scanf to skip any white space first, including that leftover newline.

Reading strings with scanf: scanf("%s", name); reads a word into a char array called name. Notice there is no & here, because an array name already acts as an address; you will see why in lesson 20. But %s stops at the first space, so typing Rahim Uddin stores only Rahim. To read a full line with spaces, use fgets(name, sizeof name, stdin);, which you will meet again in the strings lesson. Never use the old gets function; it was removed from C in the C11 standard because it could overflow the array.

Character input and output: For single characters, C has simpler functions. getchar() reads one character from the keyboard and returns it. putchar(c) prints one character. Example: char c = getchar(); putchar(c); echoes back the first key typed. puts("Hello"); prints a string and automatically adds a newline at the end. These are handy when you process text one character at a time, such as counting vowels.

A complete small program: Let us combine everything. Line 1: #include <stdio.h>. Then inside main: int a, b; printf("Enter two numbers: "); if (scanf("%d %d", &a, &b) != 2) { printf("Please type two whole numbers\n"); return 1; } printf("Sum = %d\n", a + b); printf("Product = %d\n", a * b); printf("Average = %.2f\n", (a + b) / 2.0); return 0;. If the user types 7 and 4, the output is Sum = 11, Product = 28 and Average = 5.50. If the user types hello, the program politely complains and returns 1 to signal a problem. This small pattern, prompt, read, check, calculate, print, is the skeleton of hundreds of lab exercises you will write this semester.

Characters are numbers too: Because a char is stored as a small integer, you can print it either way. char c = 'A'; printf("%c %d\n", c, c); prints A 65. And printf("%c\n", 66); prints B. This trick is useful when you want to see the code of a character, or turn a number into a letter, for example to print grades A, B, C by adding to 'A'. It also explains why scanf("%c") and scanf("%d") behave so differently: one reads a single raw character, the other reads digits and converts them into a number.

Buffered input: When you type at the keyboard, your characters do not go to the program one by one. They wait in a buffer, a small waiting area, until you press Enter. Then scanf or getchar takes what it needs from the buffer, and anything left over stays for the next read. This is exactly why the leftover newline causes the %c trap. Once you picture the buffer as a queue at a ticket counter, many confusing input bugs make sense.

Real life example 1, a bus fare calculator: A Dhaka bus helper program could ask: printf("Enter distance in km: "); scanf("%lf", &km);. Then it calculates fare = km * 2.45; and prints printf("Fare: %.2f taka\n", fare);. With 10 km, it prints Fare: 24.50 taka. Note the %lf in scanf because km is a double, and %.2f in printf to show exactly two decimals, as money should be shown. The per-kilometre rate here is just an example number.

Real life example 2, a marksheet line: A teacher's program reads a roll number and three marks: scanf("%d %d %d %d", &roll, &m1, &m2, &m3);. It then prints a neat row: printf("%05d %4d %4d %4d %6.2f\n", roll, m1, m2, m3, (m1 + m2 + m3) / 3.0);. For roll 42 with marks 80, 75 and 90, the output starts 00042, shows the marks in neat columns, and ends with the average 81.67. Dividing by 3.0 instead of 3 keeps the decimal part, a detail you will see in the next lesson.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The top mistakes are forgetting & in scanf (scanf("%d", age);), which usually crashes or corrupts memory; using %f to read a double; using the wrong specifier in printf; the leftover newline before %c; and using %s to read names with spaces. Exam questions include: what are format specifiers, list them; difference between printf and scanf; why does scanf need &; what do %5d, %-5d and %.2f do; what does printf return; and difference between getchar, putchar, puts and gets.

Recap: printf prints formatted output and scanf reads formatted input, both from stdio.h. Format specifiers like %d, %f, %lf, %c and %s must match the variable types. Width and precision, like %8.2f, make output tidy. scanf needs the address of each variable, written with &, except for strings read into arrays. Watch out for the leftover newline before %c and for %s stopping at spaces. Next, we start doing real calculations with C's operators.
key_points: printf prints formatted output; scanf reads formatted input; both are in stdio.h.
Common specifiers: %d int, %ld long, %f float/double (printf), %lf double (scanf), %c char, %s string.
Width and precision: %5d right-aligns, %-5d left-aligns, %05d pads zeros, %.2f shows 2 decimals.
scanf needs the address of a variable: scanf("%d", &x);
scanf returns how many items were read; printf returns how many characters were printed.
Use " %c" with a leading space to skip a leftover newline.
%s stops at a space; use fgets for whole lines and never use gets.
lessons.tip: Every time you write scanf, say out loud: 'specifier matches type, ampersand before the name'. That one sentence prevents most input bugs.
lessons.task: Write a program that reads your name (one word), age and CGPA, then prints them in one neat line like: Name: Rafi | Age: 19 | CGPA: 3.67. Try %8.2f and %-10s to see the alignment change.

quiz.q: Which specifier should scanf use to read a double?
quiz.explain: In scanf, %f is for float and %lf is for double.

quiz.q: What does printf("[%5d]", 42); print?
quiz.explain: %5d right-aligns the number in a 5-character field, padding with spaces on the left.

quiz.q: Why does scanf("%d", &x) need the &?
options: scanf needs the address of x so it can store the value there
It converts the input to an int
It is only needed for strings
quiz.explain: & gives the variable's address, so scanf can write the value into it.

quiz.q: After scanf("%d", &n); the next scanf("%c", &ch); seems to be skipped. Why?
options: It reads the leftover newline from the Enter key
quiz.explain: The newline left in the input buffer is read as the character; use " %c" to skip it.

quiz.q: What does printf("%.2f", 3.14159); print?
quiz.explain: %.2f prints the value rounded to two digits after the decimal point.

lessons.title: Operators and Expressions
lessons.content:
Think of a calculator. The numbers are the ingredients, but the buttons, plus, minus, times, divide, are what make anything happen. In C, the buttons are called operators. An operator is a symbol that tells the computer to do something with one or more values, which are called operands. In a + b, the operator is + and the operands are a and b. Put operators and operands together and you get an expression, like price * quantity - discount. This lesson covers the operators you will use every single day.

Expressions and their values: Every expression in C has a value. 3 + 4 has the value 7. age >= 18 has the value 1 if true and 0 if false. Even an assignment like x = 5 is an expression whose value is 5, which is why you can write a = b = 0; to set both to zero (it works right to left: b = 0 first, then a = that value). Understanding that everything produces a value helps you read C code like a sentence.

Kinds of operators: C groups operators by what they do. Arithmetic operators do maths. Relational operators compare. Logical operators combine true/false conditions. Assignment operators store values. Increment and decrement operators add or subtract one. There are also bitwise operators, the conditional operator ?:, the comma operator and sizeof. Operators are also grouped by how many operands they take: unary (one, like -x or !flag), binary (two, like a + b) and ternary (three, only ?:).

Arithmetic operators: The five arithmetic operators are + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division) and % (remainder, also called modulus). With a = 17 and b = 5: a + b is 22, a - b is 12, a * b is 85, a / b is 3, and a % b is 2. The first three behave as you expect. Division and remainder hide surprises, so let us look at them carefully.

Integer division: When both operands of / are integers, C does integer division: it throws away the fractional part. So 17 / 5 is 3, not 3.4, and 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. Since C99, the result is truncated toward zero, so -7 / 2 is -3. This is one of the most common sources of wrong answers. If you want the decimal result, at least one operand must be a floating type: 17.0 / 5 gives 3.4, and 7 / 2.0 gives 3.5. Remember the marksheet example from the last lesson: (m1 + m2 + m3) / 3.0, not / 3.

The remainder operator: % gives the remainder after integer division. 17 % 5 is 2 because 17 = 5 × 3 + 2. 10 % 2 is 0, which tells you 10 is even. % works only with integers; using it on float or double is a compile error (for floating remainders there is the fmod function in math.h). With negative numbers, the result takes the sign of the left operand: -7 % 3 is -1 and 7 % -3 is 1. In everyday code, % is used to check even or odd (n % 2), to get the last digit of a number (n % 10), and to wrap around in a cycle, like days of the week.

Digit tricks with / and %: These two operators together let you take numbers apart. For n = 1234: n % 10 gives 4, the last digit. n / 10 gives 123, the number without its last digit. Repeat: 123 % 10 is 3 and 123 / 10 is 12. By repeating in a loop you can extract every digit, which is how programs sum digits, reverse numbers or check palindromes. You will write these loops in lesson 10.

Unary minus and plus: A minus sign in front of a single value negates it: if x is 5, then -x is -5. This unary minus is different from binary subtraction, even though they use the same symbol. There is also a unary plus, which does nothing useful for numbers but exists for symmetry.

Relational operators: Relational operators compare two values and give 1 (true) or 0 (false). They are < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal), >= (greater than or equal), == (equal to) and != (not equal to). With a = 10 and b = 20: a < b is 1, a == b is 0, a != b is 1. Note that equal-to is written with two equals signs. A single = is assignment. Writing if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5) is a classic bug that we will meet again in lesson 8.

Logical operators: Logical operators combine conditions. && is logical AND: true only if both sides are true. || is logical OR: true if at least one side is true. ! is logical NOT: it flips true to false and false to true. Example: to check if a student passed both theory and lab: if (theory >= 40 && lab >= 40). To check for a weekend in Bangladesh: if (day == 5 || day == 6), if Friday is 5 and Saturday is 6. And !(age >= 18) means "not an adult". In C, any non-zero value counts as true, so !5 is 0 and !0 is 1.

Short-circuit evaluation: C evaluates && and || from left to right and stops as soon as the answer is known. In a && b, if a is false, the whole thing must be false, so b is not even evaluated. In a || b, if a is true, b is skipped. This is called short-circuit evaluation, and it is very useful for safety: if (count != 0 && total / count > 50) never divides by zero, because when count is 0 the division is skipped. It also means that if the right side has a side effect, like i++, that side effect might not happen.

Assignment operators: The simple assignment = stores the right-hand value into the left-hand variable. C also has compound assignment operators that combine an operation with assignment: x += 5 means x = x + 5; x -= 3 means x = x - 3; x *= 2 means x = x * 2; x /= 4 means x = x / 4; and x %= 3 means x = x % 3. They are shorter and make your intention clear: "increase the total by this price" becomes total += price;.

Increment and decrement: Adding or subtracting one is so common that C has special operators: ++ adds one and -- subtracts one. count++ and ++count both increase count by one. The difference appears when they are used inside a larger expression. In postfix form, x++, the expression's value is the old value, and x is increased afterwards. In prefix form, ++x, x is increased first and the expression's value is the new value.

Prefix versus postfix, step by step: Let x = 5. After y = x++; we have y = 5 and x = 6, because y got the old value. Now reset x = 5. After y = ++x; we have y = 6 and x = 6, because x was increased first. The same rule holds for --. When ++ or -- is used alone on a line, like i++;, there is no difference, which is why loops can use either form.

Do not modify twice: Expressions like i = i++; or printf("%d %d", i++, i++); or a[i] = i++; modify or use the same variable more than once without a clear order. The C standard says such code has undefined behavior: different compilers can give different answers, and none of them is "wrong". Some textbooks and viva questions still ask for the output of such lines, but the honest answer is that the result is not defined. Simply avoid writing them in real code.

The comma operator and sizeof: The comma operator evaluates its left side, throws the value away, then evaluates its right side, which becomes the result. You mostly see it in for loops, like for (i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i++, j--). Note that commas between function arguments are separators, not this operator. sizeof, which you met in lesson 4, is also an operator, not a function, which is why sizeof x without brackets works for a variable.

Real life example 1, splitting a bill: Five friends eat at a restaurant and the bill is 1,234 taka. int share = 1234 / 5; gives 246, and int left = 1234 % 5; gives 4. So each pays 246 taka, and 4 taka is left over for someone to cover. If you wanted the exact share, double share = 1234 / 5.0; gives 246.8. This one example shows integer division, remainder and floating division side by side, and why choosing the right one matters.

Real life example 2, a train ticket rule: Suppose a railway app gives a student discount if the passenger is under 26 and has a valid student ID, or if the passenger is over 65. The condition is if ((age < 26 && hasStudentId) || age > 65). The brackets make the grouping clear. If age is 70, the left part is false, but the right part is true, so the discount is given. Real apps are full of such combined conditions, and getting && and || right is what makes them fair.

Time conversion, a classic exercise: Convert 3,725 seconds into hours, minutes and seconds. hours = 3725 / 3600 gives 1. rem = 3725 % 3600 gives 125. minutes = 125 / 60 gives 2. seconds = 125 % 60 gives 5. So 3,725 seconds is 1 hour, 2 minutes and 5 seconds. The same pattern converts taka into notes (how many 500s, 100s, 50s) or days into weeks and days. This kind of problem appears in almost every first lab.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Common mistakes are expecting 7 / 2 to be 3.5, using % with doubles, writing = instead of ==, writing 10 < x < 20 (which C reads as (10 < x) < 20, always true because 0 or 1 is less than 20; the correct form is x > 10 && x < 20), and confusing x++ with ++x inside expressions. Exams ask: classify C operators; difference between / and %; difference between = and ==; prefix vs postfix with output examples; what is short-circuit evaluation; and evaluate small expressions like 17 / 5 * 2 + 17 % 5.

Recap: Operators act on operands to form expressions, and every expression has a value. Arithmetic operators include integer division and remainder, which drop fractions and give leftovers. Relational operators give 1 or 0, logical operators combine conditions with short-circuit evaluation, and compound assignment shortens updates. ++ and -- differ only in when the change is visible. Next lesson: which operator goes first when many appear together, how C converts between types, and the bitwise operators.
key_points: An operator acts on operands; together they form an expression that always has a value.
Arithmetic: + - * / %; integer / drops the fraction (7 / 2 is 3).
% gives the remainder, works only on integers, and is used for even/odd and digit tricks.
Relational operators (< > <= >= == !=) give 1 for true and 0 for false.
&& and || short-circuit: the right side is skipped when the answer is already known.
Compound assignment: x += 5 means x = x + 5.
x++ uses the old value then increases; ++x increases first then uses the new value.
Modifying a variable twice in one expression (i = i++) is undefined behavior.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a /, ask yourself: are both sides integers? That single question catches the most common wrong answer in C labs.
