quiz.explain: The inner x shadows the outer one only inside its block; outside, x is 1.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.content:
Have you ever stood between two mirrors in a shop and seen your reflection repeat smaller and smaller, again and again? Or opened a Russian doll to find a smaller doll inside, and another inside that, until you reach the tiniest doll that does not open? That is the feeling of recursion. In programming, recursion means a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until it reaches a version so small that the answer is obvious. It sounds like magic the first time, but once it clicks, it becomes one of the most elegant tools you have.

What recursion is: A recursive function is a function that calls itself, directly or through other functions. Every correct recursive function has two parts. The base case is the smallest version of the problem, answered directly without any further call; it is the tiniest doll. The recursive case breaks the problem into a smaller piece and calls the function itself on that piece, then uses its answer. Each call must move closer to the base case, otherwise the recursion never ends.

The classic: factorial: Remember n! = 1 × 2 × ... × n. Notice that n! = n × (n - 1)!. For example, 5! = 5 × 4!. That is a smaller version of the same problem. And 0! = 1 is the base case. In C: long long fact(int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1); }. Two lines capture the whole definition. Compare it with the loop version from lesson 10: both are correct, but the recursive one reads almost exactly like the maths.

Tracing fact(4): Let us follow the calls. fact(4) needs 4 × fact(3). fact(3) needs 3 × fact(2). fact(2) needs 2 × fact(1). fact(1) needs 1 × fact(0). fact(0) hits the base case and returns 1. Now the answers flow back: fact(1) returns 1 × 1 = 1, fact(2) returns 2 × 1 = 2, fact(3) returns 3 × 2 = 6, and fact(4) returns 4 × 6 = 24. Recursion has two phases: going down (making calls until the base case) and coming back up (combining the answers).

The call stack: How does the computer keep track of all these unfinished calls? Each call gets its own stack frame, as you learned in lesson 12, holding its own copy of n and the place to return to. When fact(4) calls fact(3), a new frame is pushed on top of the stack. When fact(0) returns, its frame is popped, and fact(1) continues where it left off. At the deepest point, five frames for fact(4) down to fact(0) sit on the stack at once. This is why each call can have its own n without confusion.

Stack overflow: The stack is limited in size. If recursion goes too deep, or never stops, the stack runs out of space and the program crashes with a stack overflow, often shown as a segmentation fault. The most common cause is a missing or wrong base case. For example, if you call fact(-1), n goes -1, -2, -3 and never reaches 0. A safer base case is if (n <= 1) return 1;. Always ask: does every possible input eventually reach the base case?

Fibonacci, recursively: The Fibonacci series is defined recursively: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, and fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2). In C: int fib(int n) { if (n <= 1) return n; return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); }. fib(6) gives 8. This version has two recursive calls in one function, which makes a tree of calls instead of a straight line: fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3), fib(4) calls fib(3) and fib(2), and so on.

Why naive Fibonacci is slow: That tree repeats a lot of work. fib(5) makes 15 calls in total, and fib(3) is computed twice, fib(2) three times. The number of calls grows roughly exponentially: fib(40) makes over three hundred million calls and takes noticeable time, while the simple loop from lesson 10 finishes instantly. This is a famous lesson: recursion is elegant, but a careless recursive solution can be extremely slow. Later, in algorithms courses, you will fix this with a technique called memoization, which stores results that were already computed.

GCD with recursion: Euclid's algorithm is naturally recursive: gcd(a, b) = a if b is 0, otherwise gcd(b, a % b). In C: int gcd(int a, int b) { if (b == 0) return a; return gcd(b, a % b); }. Trace gcd(48, 18): gcd(18, 12), then gcd(12, 6), then gcd(6, 0), which returns 6. Each call makes the numbers smaller, so it always reaches b = 0. This is one of the cleanest recursive functions you will ever see.

Sum of digits and power: Many loop problems have simple recursive versions. Sum of digits: int sumDigits(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return n % 10 + sumDigits(n / 10); }; sumDigits(472) is 2 + sumDigits(47) = 2 + 7 + sumDigits(4) = 2 + 7 + 4 + 0 = 13. Power: double power(double x, int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; return x * power(x, n - 1); }; power(2, 10) is 1024. A faster power uses the idea x^n = (x^(n/2))² for even n, which needs only about log₂ n calls.

Printing with recursion: Recursion can also produce output in a clever order. To print a number's digits in binary: void printBinary(int n) { if (n > 1) printBinary(n / 2); printf("%d", n % 2); }. For n = 6: printBinary(6) calls printBinary(3), which calls printBinary(1). printBinary(1) prints 1. Back in printBinary(3), it prints 3 % 2 = 1. Back in printBinary(6), it prints 6 % 2 = 0. Output: 110, which is 6 in binary. Because the printf happens after the recursive call, the digits come out in the correct order without needing an array.

Before or after the call: A tiny experiment shows how powerful the position of a statement is. void down(int n) { if (n == 0) return; printf("%d ", n); down(n - 1); } prints 3 2 1 for down(3), because each call prints before going deeper. void up(int n) { if (n == 0) return; up(n - 1); printf("%d ", n); } prints 1 2 3 for up(3), because each call waits until the deeper calls finish, then prints on the way back up. Same base case, same recursive call, just one line moved, and the order reverses. Try both; it is the quickest way to feel the two phases of recursion.

Tower of Hanoi: The most famous recursion puzzle has three pegs and n discs of different sizes stacked on the first peg, largest at the bottom. Move all discs to the third peg, moving one disc at a time and never putting a larger disc on a smaller one. The recursive idea: move the top n - 1 discs to the middle peg, move the largest disc to the target, then move the n - 1 discs from the middle onto it. In C: void hanoi(int n, char from, char to, char via) { if (n == 0) return; hanoi(n - 1, from, via, to); printf("Move disc %d from %c to %c\n", n, from, to); hanoi(n - 1, via, to, from); }. It needs 2^n - 1 moves: 7 moves for 3 discs, 1023 for 10 discs.

Direct and indirect recursion: When a function calls itself, it is direct recursion, like fact. When function A calls B and B calls A, it is indirect (or mutual) recursion. A classic toy example: isEven(n) returns 1 if n is 0, otherwise isOdd(n - 1); and isOdd(n) returns 0 if n is 0, otherwise isEven(n - 1). For indirect recursion, you need prototypes so each function knows about the other before it is defined.

Recursion versus iteration: Anything you can do with recursion, you can also do with loops, and vice versa, sometimes with an explicit stack. Recursion is often shorter and closer to the mathematical definition, and it shines for problems that are naturally self-similar: tree structures, Tower of Hanoi, divide-and-conquer sorting like merge sort and quicksort, and exploring mazes. Iteration usually uses less memory, because it does not need a stack frame for each step, and it is often faster. A good programmer picks whichever is clearer and efficient enough for the problem at hand.

How to write a recursive function: Follow three steps. First, define the problem in terms of a smaller version of itself: "sum of 1 to n is n plus the sum of 1 to n - 1". Second, find the base case: "sum of 1 to 0 is 0". Third, trust the recursion: assume the smaller call works correctly, and just combine its result. Beginners often try to trace every call in their head and get lost. Instead, check the base case, check one recursive step, and trust that the pattern holds, just like mathematical induction.

Real life example 1, folders inside folders: Your computer's file system is recursive: a folder contains files and other folders, which contain more files and folders. To compute the total size of a folder, a program does: size(folder) = sum of the sizes of its files + sum of size(subfolder) for each subfolder. The base case is a folder with no subfolders. This is exactly how "Properties" in Windows or du on Linux finds the size of a folder, walking down the tree recursively.

Real life example 2, a family tree: Think of a family tree going back many generations. To count all your ancestors up to some generation, you count your two parents, then recursively count each parent's ancestors. To find whether someone is your ancestor, you check your parents, and if not found, check their ancestors recursively. Genealogy apps, organisation charts and comment threads on Facebook (replies to replies to replies) all use this kind of recursive thinking.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: missing base case, base case that some inputs never reach (like negative numbers), forgetting to return the result of the recursive call (writing fact(n - 1); instead of return n * fact(n - 1);), recursion that does not shrink the problem, and using naive recursive Fibonacci for big n. Exams ask: define recursion with its two parts; write recursive factorial, Fibonacci, GCD, sum of digits or power; trace a recursive call and show the stack; compare recursion and iteration; explain stack overflow; and write the Tower of Hanoi with the number of moves.

Recap: Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on a smaller input until a base case answers directly. Each call has its own stack frame, so values do not mix, but too deep recursion causes a stack overflow. Factorial, GCD, sum of digits and power have short recursive forms; naive Fibonacci shows how recursion can be slow. Recursion shines on self-similar problems like Hanoi and trees. Next we move to arrays, which let one variable hold many values.
key_points: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem.
Every recursion needs a base case that returns directly and a recursive case that shrinks the problem.
fact(n) = n × fact(n - 1) with fact(0) = 1.
Each call gets its own stack frame; too deep recursion causes stack overflow.
Naive recursive Fibonacci repeats work and grows exponentially slow.
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) with gcd(a, 0) = a.
Tower of Hanoi with n discs needs 2^n - 1 moves.
Recursion is often clearer; iteration usually uses less memory.

lessons.title: One-Dimensional Arrays
lessons.content:
Suppose your class has 60 students and you want to store everyone's marks. You could declare 60 variables: marks1, marks2, marks3, all the way to marks60. Then to find the average you would write a sum with 60 terms, and if a new student joins, you edit everything. That is madness. Instead, think of an egg tray: one tray, many slots in a row, each slot numbered. In C, that egg tray is an array. One name, many values of the same type, each reached by its position number. Arrays are the first data structure you learn, and together with loops they unlock almost every real program.

What an array is: An array is a collection of elements of the same type, stored one after another in contiguous memory, and accessed by a single name plus an index. int marks[60]; creates 60 int boxes, side by side, all called marks. You reach each box with marks[0], marks[1], and so on. Because all elements have the same type and sit next to each other, the computer can jump directly to any element instantly, no matter how big the array is.

Declaring an array: The form is type name[size];. Examples: int marks[60]; double prices[10]; char grades[5];. The size must be a positive integer. In classic C (C89) it must be a constant, often written with #define SIZE 60 so that you can change it in one place. C99 also allows variable length arrays, like int a[n]; where n is read at runtime, but they became optional in C11 and many teachers prefer fixed sizes, so use constants in exams unless told otherwise.

Indexing starts at zero: The first element is at index 0, not 1. For int a[5], the valid indices are 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4. a[5] does not exist. This feels strange at first, but it comes from how addresses work: the index is the distance from the start of the array. The first element is zero steps from the start. Many bugs come from forgetting this, so say it out loud: "an array of size n has indices 0 to n - 1".

Initializing an array: You can give values when declaring: int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};. If you give fewer values than the size, the rest become 0: int b[5] = {1, 2}; gives 1, 2, 0, 0, 0. So int zeros[100] = {0}; is a quick way to set all elements to zero. If you leave out the size, C counts the values for you: int c[] = {3, 6, 9}; makes an array of size 3. A local array with no initializer at all contains garbage values, just like a local variable.

Reading and writing elements: Each element behaves like an ordinary variable. a[2] = 99; stores 99 in the third element. printf("%d", a[0]); prints the first. scanf("%d", &a[i]); reads into element i, and the & is needed because a[i] is a single int. You can use any integer expression as an index: a[i + 1], a[n - 1], a[2 * k]. The last element of an array of size n is always a[n - 1].

Traversing with a loop: The real power appears when you combine arrays with for loops. To read 5 marks: for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) scanf("%d", &marks[i]);. To print them: for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) printf("%d ", marks[i]);. Notice the pattern: start at 0, continue while i < n, increase by 1. This loop header, for (i = 0; i < n; i++), is the most common line in all of C. Using i <= n here is the classic off-by-one bug that reads one element past the end.

Sum and average: To add all elements: int sum = 0; for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i]; then double avg = (double)sum / n;. For marks 70, 85, 60, 90 and 75, sum is 380 and the average is 76.0. Notice the cast from lesson 7, so that the average keeps its decimals. These two lines appear in thousands of real programs, from class result sheets to sales reports.

Finding the maximum and minimum: Start by assuming the first element is the largest: int max = a[0]; then check the rest: for (i = 1; i < n; i++) if (a[i] > max) max = a[i];. For 70, 85, 60, 90, 75, max goes 70, 85, 85, 90, 90. The minimum is the same with <. Do not start max at 0, because if all values are negative, like temperatures in a freezer, 0 would wrongly win. You can also remember the position: if (a[i] > max) { max = a[i]; pos = i; }.

Counting and frequency: To count how many students passed: count = 0; for (i = 0; i < n; i++) if (a[i] >= 40) count++;. To count how often each value appears, use a second array as counters. For dice rolls from 1 to 6: int freq[7] = {0}; for (i = 0; i < n; i++) freq[roll[i]]++;. After the loop, freq[3] tells how many 3s were rolled. Using a value as an index into a counter array is a beautiful trick that you will use again in algorithms courses.

Reversing an array: To reverse in place, swap the first and last elements, then the second and second-last, moving inwards until the middle: for (i = 0, j = n - 1; i < j; i++, j--) { temp = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = temp; }. For 1 2 3 4 5: swap 1 and 5, then 2 and 4, and the middle 3 stays; result 5 4 3 2 1. The three-line swap with a temporary variable is a pattern you will write many times.

Inserting and deleting: Arrays have fixed size and no gaps, so inserting means shifting. To insert x at position p in an array holding n elements (with spare room): for (i = n; i > p; i--) a[i] = a[i - 1]; a[p] = x; n++;. Shifting must go from the end backwards, otherwise you overwrite values before moving them. To delete position p: for (i = p; i < n - 1; i++) a[i] = a[i + 1]; n--;. Both take time proportional to n, which is one reason later courses introduce linked lists.

How arrays sit in memory: If int a[5] starts at address 1000 and an int is 4 bytes, then a[0] is at 1000, a[1] at 1004, a[2] at 1008, and in general a[i] is at 1000 + i × 4. This formula, base address plus index times element size, is why indexing is instant and why indices start at 0. sizeof(a) gives the total bytes, 20 here, and sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) gives the number of elements, 5, a handy trick inside the function where the array is declared.

No bounds checking: C does not check whether an index is valid. If you write a[5] = 7; for an array of size 5, C will happily write into whatever memory comes after the array, possibly another variable. The result is undefined behavior: sometimes nothing visible happens, sometimes another variable mysteriously changes, sometimes the program crashes. This is one of the most dangerous bugs in C and the source of many security holes called buffer overflows. Always make sure your loop limits match the array size.

Arrays cannot be assigned directly: You cannot copy an array with =. int a[3] = {1, 2, 3}, b[3]; b = a; is a compile error. You must copy element by element: for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) b[i] = a[i];. Likewise, a == b does not compare contents; it compares addresses, as you will understand in the pointers lessons. Arrays are a bit special in C, and this is part of why.

Passing arrays to functions: You can pass an array to a function: double average(int a[], int n) { int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i]; return (double)sum / n; } and call it as average(marks, 5);. Two important facts. First, the function does not know the array's size, so you must pass n separately; sizeof inside the function gives the size of a pointer, not of the array. Second, the function works on the original array, not a copy, so if it changes a[i], the caller's array changes too. This is different from ordinary variables, and the reason is that the array name is passed as an address, which lesson 20 explains.

Using #define for the size: A good habit is to give the size a name once: #define N 60, then int marks[N]; and for (i = 0; i < N; i++). If next year the class has 65 students, you change one line and every loop follows. Hard-coding 60 in five different places invites a bug where one loop still says 60 while the array became 65. This is the same "one place for one fact" idea that makes functions and constants valuable.

Real life example 1, daily sales of a shop: A small shop in Mirpur records sales for each day of a month in double sales[31];. One loop reads the values, another finds the total, a third finds the best day with a max search that remembers the index, and a fourth counts days with sales above 10,000 taka. The owner gets a monthly summary from four small loops over one array. Spreadsheet software does exactly this kind of work, just with a nicer screen.

Real life example 2, polling votes: In a class election with 4 candidates numbered 1 to 4, each student's vote is stored in int votes[60];. A frequency array int count[5] = {0}; and one loop, count[votes[i]]++, tallies all the votes. Then a max search over count[1] to count[4] finds the winner. The same idea, values used as indices into counters, is how vote counting, survey analysis and word-frequency tools work at a much larger scale.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes include starting at index 1 and missing a[0], using i <= n and going out of bounds, forgetting to initialize sums, starting max at 0, trying to assign arrays with =, expecting sizeof to work on an array parameter, and inserting by shifting forwards. Exams ask: define an array and its advantages; how to declare and initialize; find sum, average, maximum and minimum; reverse an array; count even and odd elements; insert or delete an element; compute the address of a[i] given a base address; and how arrays are passed to functions.

Recap: An array stores many values of one type in contiguous memory under one name, indexed from 0 to n - 1. Initialize with braces; missing values become 0. Loops with for (i = 0; i < n; i++) traverse arrays to sum, average, search for max, count and reverse. C does not check bounds, so stay inside the array. Arrays cannot be copied with = and are passed to functions as addresses, so functions can change them and need the size passed separately. Next: searching and sorting, the two most famous array algorithms.
key_points: An array holds many values of one type in contiguous memory under one name.
Indices run from 0 to n - 1; a[n] is out of bounds.
int a[5] = {1, 2}; sets the rest to 0; int c[] = {3, 6, 9}; has size 3.
Traverse with for (i = 0; i < n; i++); start max/min at a[0], sums at 0.
Address of a[i] = base address + i × sizeof(element).
C does not check bounds; writing past the end is undefined behavior.
Arrays cannot be copied with =; copy element by element.
Arrays are passed to functions as addresses: changes affect the caller, and the size must be passed separately.
lessons.tip: Whenever you write a loop over an array, check two numbers out loud: the first index (0) and the last index (n - 1). It catches most array bugs before they happen.

lessons.title: Searching and Sorting Arrays
lessons.content:
Imagine looking for a friend's phone number in two different notebooks. In the first, numbers are written in random order as people gave them, so you read every line from the top until you find the name. In the second, the names are in alphabetical order, so you open the middle, see that "Rahim" comes after "Karim", and jump to the second half, again and again, finding the name in a few flips. Searching and sorting are about exactly this. Sorting puts data in order, and searching finds an item. Order makes searching dramatically faster. In this lesson you will write linear search, binary search, bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort, and trace each by hand.

Searching: Searching means finding whether a value, called the key, is present in a collection, and usually where. The answer is an index if found, or a special value like -1 if not found. We measure a search by how many comparisons it needs, because comparisons are the main work. With small arrays the method hardly matters, but with a million elements, the difference between methods is the difference between instant and painfully slow.

Linear search: The simplest method checks each element from the start until it finds the key or reaches the end. int linearSearch(int a[], int n, int key) { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (a[i] == key) return i; return -1; }. For a = {7, 3, 9, 4, 1} and key 4, it compares with 7, 3, 9, then 4 and returns index 3. For key 8, it checks all five and returns -1. Linear search works on any array, sorted or not.

Cost of linear search: In the best case, the key is the first element: 1 comparison. In the worst case, it is last or absent: n comparisons. On average, about n / 2. We say linear search takes time proportional to n, written O(n) in big-O notation, which you will study properly in the algorithms course. For 1,000,000 elements, that can mean up to a million comparisons per search.

Binary search: If the array is sorted, we can do much better. Look at the middle element. If it equals the key, done. If the key is smaller, the key can only be in the left half; if larger, only in the right half. Throw away the other half and repeat. In C: int low = 0, high = n - 1; while (low <= high) { int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; if (a[mid] == key) return mid; else if (a[mid] < key) low = mid + 1; else high = mid - 1; } return -1;.

Tracing binary search: Take the sorted array {2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91} (indices 0 to 9) and key 23. Step 1: low = 0, high = 9, mid = 4, a[4] = 16 < 23, so low = 5. Step 2: low = 5, high = 9, mid = 7, a[7] = 56 > 23, so high = 6. Step 3: low = 5, high = 6, mid = 5, a[5] = 23, found at index 5. Three comparisons instead of six. For a missing key, low eventually passes high and the loop ends with -1.

Cost of binary search: Each step halves the remaining range. Starting with n elements, after k steps about n / 2^k remain, so the number of steps is about log₂ n. For 1,000 elements that is about 10 comparisons; for 1,000,000, about 20; for a billion, about 30. This is written O(log n), and it is one of the most important speed-ups in all of computing. The price is that the data must be sorted first, which is why sorting matters so much.

The mid formula: You may see mid = (low + high) / 2 in books, and for small arrays it works. But if low and high are both very large, their sum can overflow an int. mid = low + (high - low) / 2 gives the same result without that risk. This is a famous real-world bug that hid in widely used library code for years before it was noticed, which shows how subtle even simple algorithms can be.

Sorting: Sorting means arranging elements in order, usually ascending (smallest first) or descending. There are dozens of sorting algorithms. In this course you learn the simple ones that use nested loops, take about n² comparisons, and are easy to trace: bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort. Faster ones like merge sort and quicksort, which take about n log n, come in the data structures and algorithms courses.

Bubble sort: Bubble sort repeatedly walks through the array, comparing each pair of neighbours and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. After the first pass, the largest element has "bubbled" to the end. After the second pass, the second largest is in place, and so on. for (i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) for (j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) if (a[j] > a[j + 1]) { t = a[j]; a[j] = a[j + 1]; a[j + 1] = t; }. The inner limit n - 1 - i skips the part that is already sorted.

Tracing bubble sort: Sort {5, 1, 4, 2, 8}. Pass 1: compare 5 and 1, swap: {1, 5, 4, 2, 8}; 5 and 4, swap: {1, 4, 5, 2, 8}; 5 and 2, swap: {1, 4, 2, 5, 8}; 5 and 8, no swap. Now 8 is in place. Pass 2: 1 and 4 fine; 4 and 2, swap: {1, 2, 4, 5, 8}; 4 and 5 fine. Pass 3: no swaps. Pass 4: no swaps. Sorted: {1, 2, 4, 5, 8}. Exams very often ask you to show the array after each pass, exactly like this.

Improving bubble sort: In the trace, passes 3 and 4 did nothing because the array was already sorted. An improved bubble sort keeps a flag: set swapped = 0 at the start of each pass, set it to 1 whenever a swap happens, and if a pass ends with swapped still 0, break out early. On an already sorted array this version finishes after one pass of n - 1 comparisons. In the worst case, a reverse-sorted array, it still needs about n² / 2 comparisons.

Selection sort: Selection sort finds the smallest element and puts it first, then finds the smallest of the rest and puts it second, and so on. for (i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) { min = i; for (j = i + 1; j < n; j++) if (a[j] < a[min]) min = j; if (min != i) { t = a[i]; a[i] = a[min]; a[min] = t; } }. Trace {64, 25, 12, 22, 11}: the smallest is 11, swap with 64: {11, 25, 12, 22, 64}. Next smallest from index 1 is 12, swap with 25: {11, 12, 25, 22, 64}. Next is 22, swap with 25: {11, 12, 22, 25, 64}. Then 25 is already in place. Done.

Selection versus bubble: Selection sort always makes about n² / 2 comparisons, even if the array is already sorted, but it makes at most n - 1 swaps. Bubble sort can make many more swaps. When swapping is expensive, for example moving big records, selection sort can be better. When the data is nearly sorted, improved bubble sort or insertion sort finishes faster.

Insertion sort: Insertion sort works like arranging playing cards in your hand. Take the next card and slide it left past the bigger cards until it sits in the right place. for (i = 1; i < n; i++) { key = a[i]; j = i - 1; while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) { a[j + 1] = a[j]; j--; } a[j + 1] = key; }. For {5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3}: insert 2 before 5, giving {2, 5, 4, 6, 1, 3}; insert 4 between 2 and 5; 6 stays; 1 slides to the front; 3 slides between 2 and 4. Final: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. It is very fast on nearly sorted data.

Sorting other things: The same algorithms sort any type you can compare. To sort descending, flip the comparison: a[j] < a[j + 1] in bubble sort. To sort characters, compare their codes. To sort names, compare strings with strcmp, which you meet in lesson 18. To sort student records by marks, compare the marks field and swap the whole records, which you will do with structures in lesson 22. The C standard library also has qsort in stdlib.h, a general sorting function you can use once you understand function pointers in later courses.

Real life example 1, a phone contact list: Your phone keeps contacts sorted by name. When you type "Ra", it can binary-search to the first name starting with "Ra" in a list of a thousand contacts in about ten steps. When you add a new contact, it is inserted into the right place, like one step of insertion sort. If the contacts were not sorted, every search would mean scanning the whole list. Sorting once and searching many times is a pattern you will see everywhere.

Real life example 2, a merit list: After an admission test, a university must publish a merit list sorted by score. With a few hundred applicants, even a simple sort finishes in a blink. With hundreds of thousands, as in large national admission tests, the program must use a fast n log n algorithm, because n² comparisons would take far too long. Then, when a student checks their position by roll number on the website, the system uses a fast search rather than reading every record. This is the same theory as this lesson, at national scale.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: using binary search on an unsorted array, getting the low/high updates wrong (mid instead of mid + 1, causing infinite loops), wrong inner loop limits in bubble sort that read a[n], forgetting the temporary variable in a swap (a[j] = a[j + 1]; a[j + 1] = a[j]; loses a value), and confusing selection and bubble sort. Exams ask: write linear and binary search; trace binary search for a key; show each pass of bubble or selection sort; compare their comparisons and swaps; explain why binary search needs sorted data; and state the time complexity of each.

Recap: Linear search checks every element and works on any array in O(n). Binary search halves a sorted range each step and needs only about log₂ n comparisons. Bubble sort swaps neighbours so the largest bubbles to the end; selection sort picks the minimum each round with few swaps; insertion sort slides each new element into place and is fast on nearly sorted data. All three take about n² comparisons in the worst case. Next: two-dimensional arrays, where data has rows and columns.
key_points: Linear search checks each element in turn; works on unsorted data; up to n comparisons.
Binary search needs sorted data and halves the range each step: about log2(n) comparisons.
Use mid = low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid overflow.
Bubble sort swaps adjacent elements; after pass k the k largest are in place.
A swapped flag lets bubble sort stop early on sorted data.
Selection sort picks the minimum each round and makes at most n - 1 swaps.
Insertion sort slides each element into place and is fast on nearly sorted data.
Simple sorts take about n^2 comparisons; merge sort and quicksort are faster (n log n).
lessons.tip: Practise sorting with five small numbered paper slips on your desk. Physically doing a bubble pass or a selection round makes exam traces easy.
lessons.task: Sort {29, 10, 14, 37, 13} by hand with bubble sort and with selection sort, writing the array after every pass. Then binary-search the sorted result for 14 and for 30, writing low, high and mid at each step.

quiz.q: What does binary search require?
options: The array must have an even size
The key must be at the middle
The array must contain no zeros
quiz.explain: Binary search discards halves based on order, so the data must be sorted.

quiz.q: About how many comparisons does binary search need for 1,000,000 sorted elements?
quiz.explain: log2(1,000,000) is about 20.

quiz.q: After the first pass of bubble sort (ascending), which element is guaranteed in its final place?
quiz.explain: Each pass bubbles the largest remaining element to the end.

quiz.q: Selection sort on {64, 25, 12, 22, 11}: what is the array after the first swap?
quiz.explain: The minimum 11 is swapped with the first element 64.

quiz.q: Which simple sort makes at most n - 1 swaps?
quiz.explain: Selection sort does one swap per round at most.

lessons.title: Two-Dimensional Arrays and Matrices
lessons.content:
Look at your class routine pinned on the notice board. Days go down the side, periods go across the top, and each box holds one subject. To find what you have on Tuesday in the third period, you go to the Tuesday row and the third column. That grid is a two-dimensional array. A one-dimensional array is a single row of boxes; a two-dimensional array is a table of rows and columns. Spreadsheets, chess boards, cinema seats, images made of pixels and mathematical matrices are all 2D arrays. In this lesson you will learn to declare them, fill them, walk through them with nested loops, and do the classic matrix operations.

What a 2D array is: A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays: each row is itself a one-dimensional array, and all rows have the same length and type. int m[3][4]; declares 3 rows and 4 columns, which is 12 int elements in total. The first index chooses the row and the second chooses the column, so m[1][2] is the element in row 1, column 2. As with 1D arrays, both indices start at 0, so rows run 0 to 2 and columns 0 to 3 here.

Declaring and initializing: The general form is type name[rows][cols];. You can initialize row by row with nested braces: int m[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};. Row 0 is 1 2 3 and row 1 is 4 5 6. You can also write the values in one flat list, int m[2][3] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};, and C fills them row by row, but the nested form is clearer. Missing values become 0, so int z[3][3] = {0}; makes an all-zero matrix. You may leave out the number of rows, int m[][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};, but never the number of columns.

Accessing elements: m[i][j] behaves like any variable. m[0][0] = 10; sets the top-left corner. printf("%d", m[1][2]); prints the element in row 1, column 2. scanf("%d", &m[i][j]); reads into a single element. Notice the syntax: two separate pairs of brackets. Writing m[1, 2] is a mistake that compiles in a confusing way, because the comma operator makes it mean m[2], a whole row.

Traversing with nested loops: To visit every element, use a nested loop: the outer loop over rows, the inner loop over columns. Reading: for (i = 0; i < R; i++) for (j = 0; j < C; j++) scanf("%d", &m[i][j]);. Printing as a table: for (i = 0; i < R; i++) { for (j = 0; j < C; j++) printf("%4d", m[i][j]); printf("\n"); }. This is the same row-then-column pattern you used for the multiplication table in lesson 11.

Row-major storage: Memory is a single long line of bytes, so how does a table fit? C stores 2D arrays in row-major order: all of row 0 first, then all of row 1, and so on. For int m[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}}, memory holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 in that order. This is why the column count must be known: to find m[i][j], C skips i full rows of C elements and then j more elements.

Address calculation: The address of m[i][j] is base + (i × C + j) × size, where C is the number of columns and size is the size of one element. For int m[3][4] starting at address 1000, with 4-byte ints, m[2][1] is at 1000 + (2 × 4 + 1) × 4 = 1000 + 36 = 1036. Exams often ask this. (Some languages, such as Fortran, use column-major order instead, but C is always row-major.)

Row sums and column sums: To sum each row: for (i = 0; i < R; i++) { sum = 0; for (j = 0; j < C; j++) sum += m[i][j]; printf("Row %d: %d\n", i, sum); }. To sum each column, swap the loop roles: the outer loop over columns, the inner over rows, adding m[i][j]. For a marks table where rows are students and columns are subjects, row sums give each student's total, and column sums give each subject's class total.

Square matrices and diagonals: A matrix with the same number of rows and columns is square. Its main diagonal has elements where i == j: m[0][0], m[1][1], m[2][2]. The sum of the main diagonal, called the trace, is for (i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += m[i][i];, a single loop. The other diagonal has elements where i + j == N - 1, so its sum is for (i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += m[i][N - 1 - i];. The identity matrix has 1 on the main diagonal and 0 elsewhere: m[i][j] = (i == j) ? 1 : 0;.

Matrix addition: Two matrices can be added only if they have the same dimensions. Each element of the result is the sum of the matching elements: c[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j];, inside the usual nested loop. For a = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}} and b = {{5, 6}, {7, 8}}, c = {{6, 8}, {10, 12}}. Subtraction works the same way with minus. Always check the dimensions first and print an error if they do not match.

Transpose: The transpose of a matrix turns rows into columns: t[j][i] = m[i][j]. An R × C matrix becomes a C × R matrix. For m = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}}, the transpose is {{1, 4}, {2, 5}, {3, 6}}. A square matrix is symmetric if it equals its own transpose, which you can check with a nested loop that looks for any m[i][j] != m[j][i]. To transpose a square matrix in place, swap m[i][j] with m[j][i] only for j > i, otherwise every pair is swapped twice and nothing changes.

Matrix multiplication, the rule: Multiplying matrix A (r1 × c1) by matrix B (r2 × c2) is possible only if c1 == r2, the columns of A equal the rows of B. The result C is r1 × c2. Each element C[i][j] is the sum, over k, of A[i][k] × B[k][j]: row i of A multiplied element by element with column j of B, then added. Unlike ordinary numbers, matrix multiplication is not commutative: A × B is usually not equal to B × A, and one of them may not even be defined.

Matrix multiplication, the code and a worked example: for (i = 0; i < r1; i++) for (j = 0; j < c2; j++) { C[i][j] = 0; for (k = 0; k < c1; k++) C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j]; }. Three nested loops. Example: A = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}} and B = {{5, 6}, {7, 8}}. C[0][0] = 1 × 5 + 2 × 7 = 19. C[0][1] = 1 × 6 + 2 × 8 = 22. C[1][0] = 3 × 5 + 4 × 7 = 43. C[1][1] = 3 × 6 + 4 × 8 = 50. So C = {{19, 22}, {43, 50}}. Forgetting C[i][j] = 0 before the k loop is the most common bug here.

Searching a 2D array: To find a value in a table, walk it with the usual nested loop and stop when found. Because break only exits the inner loop, use a flag or put the search in a function that returns the position as soon as it finds the key. For a seat map, the function might return the row and column through two variables, which needs pointers from lesson 20, or it can return a single number like row × C + col, from which you recover the row with / C and the column with % C. That last trick is exactly the row-major formula used backwards.

Cost of matrix operations: Addition and transpose of an n × n matrix take about n² steps. The simple multiplication takes about n³ multiplications: for n = 100, that is a million; for n = 1000, a billion. That is why scientists and game engines use highly optimised libraries and graphics cards for matrix work. Later courses in numerical methods, graphics and machine learning are full of matrices.

Passing 2D arrays to functions: When a function receives a 2D array, it must know the number of columns, so that it can compute addresses. The parameter is written like void printMatrix(int m[][4], int rows). The first dimension may be left empty, but the second must be given. As with 1D arrays, the function works on the original array, not a copy. With C99 variable length arrays you can write void f(int r, int c, int m[r][c]), but fixed column sizes with #define are the safe exam choice.

Higher dimensions and arrays of strings: C allows more dimensions: int cube[2][3][4]; has 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 elements, and you need three nested loops to walk it. They are less common but useful, for example for colour images (height × width × 3 colour channels). A very common 2D array is a list of strings: char names[5][20]; holds five names of up to 19 characters each, which you will use after the strings lesson.

Real life example 1, a classroom marksheet: A teacher stores marks of 40 students in 5 subjects as int marks[40][5];. Row sums give each student's total and allow the merit position. Column averages show which subject was hardest. A search through the table finds any mark below 40 to list students who need help. This one table, with a few nested loops, gives the whole result analysis that schools in Bangladesh do every term.

Real life example 2, a digital photo: A black-and-white photo is a 2D array of brightness values from 0 (black) to 255 (white). To make it brighter, add 30 to each pixel, capping at 255. To flip it left to right, swap m[i][j] with m[i][W - 1 - j] across each row. To rotate it, you combine a transpose with a flip. Photo apps on your phone do these exact operations, just on millions of pixels and with colour channels.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: swapping row and column indices, writing m[i, j], leaving out the column size in a function parameter, forgetting to reset C[i][j] = 0 in multiplication, multiplying incompatible matrices, transposing a square matrix in place by swapping all pairs (which undoes itself), and loop limits that use rows where columns belong. Exams ask: declare and initialize a 2D array; explain row-major order and compute an element's address; write programs for matrix addition, transpose and multiplication; find diagonal sums; check symmetric or identity matrices; and explain how a 2D array is passed to a function.

Recap: A 2D array is a table of rows and columns, declared as type name[rows][cols] and accessed as m[i][j], both indices starting at 0. C stores it row by row, so address = base + (i × cols + j) × size. Nested loops traverse it. Matrix addition needs equal dimensions; multiplication needs columns of A to equal rows of B and uses three loops. Functions receiving 2D arrays need the column size. Next we look at a special kind of character array: strings.
key_points: A 2D array is a table: int m[R][C] has R rows and C columns, indexed from 0.
Initialize row by row: int m[2][3] = {{1,2,3},{4,5,6}}; the column size can never be omitted.
C stores 2D arrays in row-major order: row 0, then row 1, and so on.
Address of m[i][j] = base + (i × C + j) × element size.
Main diagonal: i == j; other diagonal: i + j == N - 1.
Addition needs equal sizes; transpose swaps rows and columns.
A (r1×c1) × B (r2×c2) needs c1 == r2, gives r1×c2, and uses C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j].
Functions must know the column count: void f(int m[][4], int rows).
lessons.tip: Before coding any matrix operation, draw the matrices as boxes on paper and compute one result element by hand. If you can do C[0][1] by hand, the code is just loops around it.
lessons.task: Write a program that reads two 3 × 3 matrices and prints their sum, the transpose of the first, and their product. Check C[0][0] of the product by hand.

quiz.q: How many elements does int m[3][4] have?
quiz.explain: 3 rows × 4 columns = 12 elements.

quiz.q: In what order does C store a 2D array?
quiz.explain: C stores all of row 0, then row 1, and so on.

quiz.q: int m[3][4] starts at 1000, int is 4 bytes. Address of m[2][1]?
A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 4. What is the size of A × B?
quiz.explain: Columns of A (3) equal rows of B (3), and the result is rows of A × columns of B = 2 × 4.

quiz.q: Which function parameter for a 2D array is valid?
quiz.explain: The column size must be given so the function can compute element addresses.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.content:
Your name, a text message, a bKash transaction ID, a song title, a password: so much of the information we deal with every day is text. In C, text is stored as a string. But C has no special string type like some other languages. A C string is simply an array of characters with a special invisible marker at the end that says "the text stops here". Once you understand that one idea, everything about strings in C makes sense, including why they are powerful and why they cause so many bugs. This lesson covers how strings are stored, how to read and print them, the string.h library, and the classic string programs.

What a string is: In C, a string is a sequence of characters stored in a char array and terminated by the null character, written '\0', whose value is 0. The word "Dhaka" is stored as six bytes: 'D', 'h', 'a', 'k', 'a', '\0'. The terminator is how every string function knows where the text ends, because the array itself does not carry its length. Without '\0', a char array is just a bunch of characters, not a proper string.

Declaring strings: char city[6] = "Dhaka"; reserves 6 bytes: 5 letters plus the terminator. If you write char city[] = "Dhaka";, C counts for you and makes the size 6. You can also make room for longer text: char name[50]; holds up to 49 characters plus '\0'. Writing char city[5] = "Dhaka"; leaves no room for '\0' (C allows this in initialization but the result is not a valid string), a classic trap. Always size a string buffer as "longest text plus one".

Character-by-character initialization: char word[] = {'H', 'i', '\0'}; is the same as char word[] = "Hi";. The double-quoted form adds the '\0' automatically; the brace form does not, so you must add it yourself. Remember from lesson 3 that 'A' is a single character while "A" is a string of two bytes, 'A' and '\0'.

Printing strings: printf("%s\n", city); prints characters starting at city[0] and stops at '\0'. puts(city); prints the string and adds a newline. You can also print character by character: for (i = 0; city[i] != '\0'; i++) putchar(city[i]);. That loop condition, keep going until the terminator, is the heart of almost every string program you will write.

Reading strings with scanf: scanf("%s", name); reads one word. There is no & before name, because an array name already gives the address of its first element. But scanf %s has two problems. It stops at the first space, so "Abdul Karim" gives only "Abdul". And it does not know the array size, so a long input can overflow the array. Writing a width limit helps: scanf("%49s", name); for a 50-byte array reads at most 49 characters.

Reading lines with fgets: To read a whole line, including spaces, use fgets(name, sizeof name, stdin);. It reads up to sizeof name - 1 characters or until a newline, and always adds '\0'. One detail: if the newline fits, fgets keeps it in the string, so "Abdul Karim\n" is stored. To remove it, a common line is name[strcspn(name, "\n")] = '\0';, where strcspn from string.h finds the position of the newline. Also remember from lesson 5 that a scanf of a number leaves a newline behind, which a following fgets would read as an empty line. Never use gets: it was removed from the language because it cannot limit the input size.

Strings are not assigned with =: Because strings are arrays, you cannot assign one to another with =. char a[20], b[20] = "Hello"; a = b; is an error, and so is a = "Hello"; after declaration. You must copy the characters, usually with strcpy(a, b);. Likewise, a == b compares addresses, not text, so it is almost always false even if both hold "Hello". Use strcmp to compare contents. Many beginner bugs come from treating strings like numbers.

The string.h library: The header string.h gives ready-made string functions. The most important are: strlen(s), the number of characters before '\0'; strcpy(dest, src), copies src into dest; strcat(dest, src), appends src to the end of dest; strcmp(a, b), compares two strings; strchr(s, c), finds a character; and strstr(s, t), finds a substring. There are safer variants with a length limit, like strncpy, strncat and strncmp, and you will see them in professional code.

strlen: strlen("Dhaka") is 5, not 6, because it does not count '\0'. sizeof is different: for char city[20] = "Dhaka";, strlen(city) is 5 while sizeof(city) is 20, the whole array. Writing strlen yourself is a classic exercise: int len = 0; while (s[len] != '\0') len++;. Each call to strlen walks the whole string, so do not call it in a loop condition on every iteration for long strings; store it in a variable once.

strcpy and strcat: strcpy(dest, "Chattogram"); copies the 10 letters and the '\0' into dest. strcat(greeting, " World"); turns "Hello" into "Hello World". Neither function checks that dest is big enough. If dest is too small, they write past the end, a buffer overflow, exactly like the out-of-bounds arrays in lesson 15. Always make sure the destination has room for the result plus '\0'.

strcmp: strcmp(a, b) compares two strings character by character using their codes. It returns 0 if they are equal, a negative value if a comes before b, and a positive value if a comes after b. So strcmp("apple", "banana") is negative, strcmp("cat", "cat") is 0, and strcmp("Zebra", "apple") is negative, because uppercase letters have smaller ASCII codes than lowercase ones. To check equality, write if (strcmp(a, b) == 0), not if (strcmp(a, b)), which means "not equal". strcmp is what you use to sort names alphabetically.

Searching inside strings: strchr(s, '@') looks for the first '@' in s and tells you where it is, or gives NULL if there is none; a quick email sanity check might start with exactly that. strstr(s, "Dhaka") looks for a whole word inside s, so strstr("Welcome to Dhaka", "Dhaka") finds it at position 11. Both return a pointer into the original string rather than an index, which will make full sense after the next two lessons. For now, comparing the result with NULL is enough to answer "is it there?".

Character functions from ctype.h: Many string tasks work on one character at a time, and ctype.h helps. isalpha(c) checks for a letter, isdigit(c) for a digit, isspace(c) for white space, isupper(c) and islower(c) for case, and toupper(c) and tolower(c) convert case. To make a whole string uppercase: for (i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++) s[i] = toupper(s[i]);. Doing it by hand also works, using the ASCII trick from lesson 7: if (s[i] >= 'a' && s[i] <= 'z') s[i] = s[i] - 'a' + 'A';.

Counting vowels and words: To count vowels: for (i = 0; s[i]; i++) { c = tolower(s[i]); if (c == 'a' || c == 'e' || c == 'i' || c == 'o' || c == 'u') count++; }. Note that s[i] alone works as the condition, because '\0' is 0, which is false. To count words, count the places where a non-space character follows a space or the start of the string. For "I love Bangladesh" that gives 3. These small programs are lab favourites.

Reversing and palindromes: To reverse a string in place, swap from both ends towards the middle, like reversing an array: for (i = 0, j = strlen(s) - 1; i < j; i++, j--) { t = s[i]; s[i] = s[j]; s[j] = t; }. "Dhaka" becomes "akahD". A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like "madam" or "level". Check it by comparing s[i] with s[j] from both ends and stopping at the first mismatch, without even reversing. Note that strrev, which some old books use, is not part of standard C, so write your own.

Converting between strings and numbers: The text "123" is not the number 123: it is the bytes '1', '2', '3', '\0'. To convert, stdlib.h offers atoi("123") giving the int 123 and atof("3.5") giving 3.5, and the more careful strtol and strtod, which can report errors. You can also convert by hand: num = 0; for (i = 0; s[i]; i++) num = num * 10 + (s[i] - '0');. The expression s[i] - '0' turns a digit character into its value, because the digit codes are consecutive. In the other direction, sprintf(buf, "%d", 123) writes a number into a string.

Arrays of strings: A list of names is a 2D char array: char names[5][20];, five strings of up to 19 characters each. names[2] is the third name, and names[2][0] is its first letter. You can read them with a loop of fgets or scanf("%19s", names[i]). To sort names, use any sorting algorithm from lesson 16 with strcmp to compare and strcpy (through a temporary buffer) to swap. This is how a class list gets printed in alphabetical order.

Real life example 1, a mobile number checker: A form on a Bangladeshi website asks for a mobile number. The program reads it as a string, checks that strlen is 11, that every character passes isdigit, and that it starts with "01" (strncmp(num, "01", 2) == 0). Storing the number as a string, not an int, keeps the leading zero and avoids overflow, which is why phone numbers, NID numbers and account numbers are almost always strings in software.

Real life example 2, a username and password check: A login program compares the typed username with the stored one using strcmp, and only if they match, compares the password. It reads both with fgets and removes the newline, otherwise "admin\n" would never equal "admin". Real systems never store plain passwords, they store hashes, which you will learn about in security courses, but the string comparison logic is the same. Forgetting the newline or using == are the two bugs that make students' login programs reject correct passwords.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: forgetting room for '\0', using = to assign or == to compare strings, using & with %s in scanf, reading names with spaces using %s, keeping fgets's newline, overflowing a buffer with strcpy or strcat, and treating strlen and sizeof as the same. Exams ask: what is a string and the null character; difference between a character array and a string; explain strlen, strcpy, strcat and strcmp with examples; write your own strlen or string copy; count vowels, words or characters; reverse a string; check a palindrome; and convert a string to uppercase.

Recap: A C string is a char array ending with '\0'. Size buffers as length plus one. Print with %s or puts, read words with scanf("%s") and lines with fgets, never gets. Strings cannot be assigned with = or compared with ==; use strcpy and strcmp from string.h, along with strlen and strcat, and watch buffer sizes. ctype.h helps with character tests and case changes. Loops until '\0' power every classic string program. Next we finally open the box behind arrays and strings: pointers.
key_points: A C string is a char array terminated by the null character '\0'.
"Dhaka" needs 6 bytes: 5 letters plus '\0'; size buffers as length + 1.
scanf("%s", s) reads one word with no &; use a width like %49s to avoid overflow.
fgets(s, sizeof s, stdin) reads a whole line and keeps the newline; never use gets.
Use strcpy to copy and strcmp to compare; = and == do not work on strings.
strlen counts characters before '\0'; sizeof gives the whole array size.
strcmp returns 0 when equal, negative if the first comes earlier, positive if later.
ctype.h: isalpha, isdigit, isspace, toupper, tolower.
lessons.tip: Whenever you draw a string on paper, always draw the '\0' box at the end. Most string bugs are about that one invisible box.
lessons.task: Write a program that reads a full line with fgets, removes the newline, and prints: its length (your own loop, not strlen), the number of vowels, the number of words, the string in uppercase, and whether it is a palindrome.

quiz.q: How many bytes does char s[] = "Dhaka"; use?
quiz.explain: 5 characters plus the terminating '\0'.

quiz.q: What does strcmp("cat", "cat") return?
quiz.explain: strcmp returns 0 when the strings are equal.

quiz.q: Which correctly copies the string b into a?
quiz.explain: Arrays cannot be assigned; strcpy copies the characters including '\0'.

quiz.q: If the user types Abdul Karim, what does scanf("%s", name) store?
quiz.explain: %s stops reading at the first white space.

quiz.q: For char s[20] = "Hi";, what are strlen(s) and sizeof(s)?
quiz.explain: strlen counts characters before '\0'; sizeof gives the array size.

lessons.title: Pointer Basics
lessons.content:
Think of your home address: house 12, road 5, Dhanmondi. The address is not your house; it is a small piece of information that tells anyone exactly where your house is. With the address, a courier from Pathao or a friend can find your house, deliver something to it, or even change what is inside (if you let them in). In C, every variable lives in memory at some address, and a pointer is a variable that stores such an address. Pointers are the most famous, most feared and most powerful feature of C. In this lesson we take them slowly: what an address is, how to make a pointer, how to use it, and how pointer arithmetic works.

Memory and addresses: The computer's main memory is like a very long street of numbered houses, each holding one byte. Every byte has a unique number called its address. When you declare int x = 25;, the compiler reserves 4 bytes (on a typical system) for x, say at addresses 1000 to 1003, and stores 25 there. The address of x is the address of its first byte, 1000 in this example. Real addresses are large numbers usually printed in hexadecimal, like 0x7ffd5e8c, and they change from run to run, so we use small made-up numbers to explain.

The address-of operator: The unary & operator gives the address of a variable. &x means "the address of x". You have used it since lesson 5: scanf("%d", &x) gives scanf the address so it can write into x. You can print an address with %p: printf("%p\n", (void *)&x);. The (void *) cast is the strictly correct way to pass an address to %p. The output looks like 0x7ffd5e8c, a hexadecimal address.

Declaring a pointer: A pointer variable is declared with a * between the type and the name: int *p;. Read it as "p is a pointer to int", meaning p can hold the address of an int. double *q; can hold the address of a double, and char *c; the address of a char. The type matters because it tells C what kind of value lives at that address and how many bytes to read. Note that in int *p, q; only p is a pointer and q is a plain int; to declare two pointers write int *p, *q;.

Pointing a pointer: To make p point to x, store x's address in it: int x = 25; int *p = &x;. Now p holds 1000 (in our example), and we say "p points to x". Drawing helps: draw a box for x with 25 inside, a box for p with an arrow from p to x. Pointers are much easier when you draw these arrows. The pointer itself is also a variable, so it has its own address too: &p is the address of the box p.

Dereferencing: The unary * operator in an expression means "the value at the address stored in". This is called dereferencing or indirection. With p = &x, *p is 25. printf("%d", *p); prints 25. And *p = 40; stores 40 at the address in p, which is x, so now x is 40. You changed x without writing its name, only through the pointer. This is the key power that makes call by reference possible in the next lesson.

The two meanings of *: The star has different meanings in different places, which confuses beginners. In a declaration, int *p, it says p is a pointer. In an expression, *p, it means "go to the address and use the value there". And between two values, a * b, it is multiplication. Similarly, & means "address of" when it is in front of a single variable, and bitwise AND when it is between two values. Read the context carefully.

A full worked example: int x = 10, y = 20; int *p = &x; *p = *p + 5; p = &y; *p = *p * 2;. Step by step: p points to x; *p + 5 is 15, stored in x, so x = 15. Then p is changed to point to y. *p * 2 is 40, stored in y, so y = 40. At the end, x is 15, y is 40, and p points to y. Tracing such code with box-and-arrow drawings is a standard exam question.

Pointer size: A pointer stores an address, so its size depends on the system, not on the type it points to. On a typical 64-bit computer, sizeof(int *), sizeof(char *) and sizeof(double *) are all 8 bytes; on older 32-bit systems they are 4 bytes. So a pointer to a single char and a pointer to a big double are the same size. What differs is how *p reads memory: one byte for a char pointer, eight bytes for a double pointer.

NULL pointers: A pointer that points to nothing is set to NULL, a special value defined in stdio.h, stdlib.h and other headers. int *p = NULL; says "p does not point anywhere yet". Dereferencing a NULL pointer is undefined behavior and usually crashes the program immediately with a segmentation fault, which is actually helpful, because the bug shows up quickly. Good practice: initialize pointers to NULL if you have no address yet, and check if (p != NULL) before using a pointer that might be empty. Many library functions return NULL to signal failure, as you will see with malloc and fopen.

Wild pointers: A pointer declared without initialization, like int *p; inside a function, contains a garbage address, just like an uninitialized int contains a garbage number. It is called a wild pointer. Writing *p = 5; then writes 5 to some random place in memory, which may corrupt other data or crash. This is one of the most dangerous bugs in C. The rule is simple: never dereference a pointer until you have given it a valid address.

Pointer types must match: int x; double *d = &x; is wrong, because d would read 8 bytes as a double where only a 4-byte int lives. Compilers warn about such mismatches. There is one special pointer type, void *, a generic pointer that can hold the address of any type. You cannot dereference a void * directly; you must first convert it to a specific type, like (int *)vp. void * is used by functions such as malloc that do not know what type you will store.

Pointer arithmetic: You can add an integer to a pointer, and the result moves by whole elements, not bytes. If p is an int pointer holding 1000, and int is 4 bytes, then p + 1 is 1004, p + 2 is 1008, and p + 3 is 1012. For a char pointer, c + 1 moves one byte; for a double pointer, d + 1 moves eight bytes. C multiplies by the size of the pointed type automatically. This is exactly why pointer type matters, and why pointers and arrays fit together so well.

Increment, decrement and subtraction: p++ moves p to the next element, and p-- to the previous one. If p and q point into the same array, q - p gives the number of elements between them, not the number of bytes. For example, if p points to a[1] and q to a[4], then q - p is 3. You can also compare pointers into the same array with <, >, == and !=. Adding two pointers, multiplying or dividing pointers makes no sense and is not allowed.

A preview with an array: int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; int *p = &a[0];. Then *p is 10, *(p + 1) is 20, *(p + 4) is 50. Moving the pointer walks through the array: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) printf("%d ", *(p + i)); prints all five values. The next lesson explains that the array name a itself behaves like &a[0], and that a[i] is actually defined as *(a + i).

Precedence traps: *p++ and (*p)++ are different. Because postfix ++ binds tighter than *, *p++ means *(p++): use the value at p, then move p to the next element. (*p)++ means increase the value that p points to, and p does not move. Similarly, *p + 1 is "the value plus one", while *(p + 1) is "the value of the next element". Add brackets whenever you are unsure, as lesson 7 advised.

Pointers to pointers: Since a pointer is a variable with its own address, you can have a pointer to a pointer: int **pp = &p;. Then *pp is p (an address), and **pp is x (the value). Double pointers appear when a function must change a pointer, and with arrays of strings. Lesson 20 shows them in use; for now, the box-and-arrow drawing simply gets one more arrow.

Real life example 1, a parcel locker: Think of the parcel lockers some delivery services use. Your parcel sits in locker 47, and you receive an SMS with the number 47. The SMS is the pointer: it is not the parcel, but it tells you where the parcel is. Going to locker 47 and opening it is dereferencing. If the SMS had a wrong or empty number, like a wild or NULL pointer, you would open the wrong locker or nothing at all. And if someone changes what is inside locker 47, everyone holding the number 47 sees the change.

Real life example 2, a shared Google Sheet link: When your group shares a single Google Sheet link instead of emailing copies of a file, everyone holds the address of the same sheet. If one person edits a cell, everyone sees the change, because they all point to the same data. Emailing copies is like call by value: each person edits a separate copy. Sharing the link is like passing a pointer. This is exactly the difference you will exploit in the next lesson to let functions change the caller's variables.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: dereferencing an uninitialized or NULL pointer, mixing pointer types, writing int *p, q; and expecting two pointers, confusing *p++ with (*p)++, printing an address with %d instead of %p, and assuming pointer arithmetic counts bytes. Exams ask: what is a pointer and why use it; explain & and * with an example; trace a short program with pointers and give the output; what is a NULL pointer and a wild pointer; explain pointer arithmetic with addresses (if p is 1000 and int is 4 bytes, what is p + 3?); and what is a pointer to pointer.

Recap: Every variable has an address. A pointer stores an address; & gives an address, and * in an expression follows it to the value. Declare with type *name, initialize with a real address or NULL, and never dereference wild or NULL pointers. Pointer size depends on the system, but pointer type decides how memory is read and how far p + 1 moves. Pointer arithmetic counts elements. Next lesson: pointers with arrays and functions, including call by reference.
key_points: Every variable has a memory address; & gives the address of a variable.
A pointer stores an address: int *p = &x; means p points to x.
*p (dereference) reads or writes the value at that address: *p = 40 changes x.
Initialize pointers; use NULL for 'points nowhere' and never dereference NULL or wild pointers.
Pointer size depends on the system (often 8 bytes on 64-bit), not on the pointed type.
p + 1 moves by one element: for an int pointer at 1000 with 4-byte ints, p + 1 is 1004.
*p++ moves the pointer; (*p)++ increases the value pointed to.
Print addresses with %p (cast to void *).
lessons.tip: Draw every pointer problem as boxes and arrows: a box for each variable with its value, and an arrow from each pointer to the box it points to. Update the drawing line by line.
lessons.task: Write a program with int x = 7 and int *p = &x. Print x, &x, p, *p and &p. Then set *p = 99 and print x again. Draw the boxes and arrows on paper before running it.

quiz.q: If int x = 25; int *p = &x; what is *p?
quiz.explain: *p follows the address in p to the value stored there, which is 25.

quiz.q: After int x = 5; int *p = &x; *p = 9; what is x?
quiz.explain: Writing through the pointer changes the variable it points to.

quiz.q: p is an int pointer holding 1000 and int is 4 bytes. What is p + 3?
quiz.explain: Pointer arithmetic moves by elements: 1000 + 3 × 4 = 1012.

quiz.q: What is dangerous about int *p; *p = 5; inside a function?
options: p is a wild pointer with a garbage address
quiz.explain: An uninitialized local pointer holds a garbage address; writing through it is undefined behavior.

quiz.q: What does (*p)++ do?
options: Moves p to the next element
Increases the value p points to
quiz.explain: The brackets make it increment the pointed-to value, not the pointer.

lessons.title: Pointers with Arrays and Functions
lessons.content:
In the last lesson you learned what a pointer is. Now comes the payoff. Remember the shared Google Sheet link: instead of sending copies, you send the address, and whoever has it can read and change the original. Pointers let C functions do exactly that. They also explain the mysteries we left open: why scanf needs &, why arrays passed to functions can be changed, and why arrays and pointers seem to be almost the same thing. In this lesson we connect pointers to arrays and to functions, write the famous swap function, and learn the const rules that keep pointers safe.

The array name as a pointer: In almost every expression, the name of an array is automatically converted to a pointer to its first element. So for int a[5], the expression a means &a[0]. That is why scanf("%s", name) needs no & for a char array: name already is an address. It is also why int *p = a; is perfectly legal and makes p point to a[0], without writing &.

Indexing is pointer arithmetic: C defines a[i] as *(a + i). The array name gives the address of element 0, adding i moves i elements forward (pointer arithmetic from lesson 19), and * reads the value there. So a[3] and *(a + 3) are exactly the same. With int *p = a;, you can also write p[3], which means *(p + 3). Because addition is commutative, even 3[a] is legal C and means the same as a[3], a fun trivia question, though nobody should write it in real code.

Walking an array with a pointer: You can traverse an array by moving a pointer instead of using an index: for (int *p = a; p < a + 5; p++) printf("%d ", *p);. Here a + 5 is the address just past the last element, which C allows you to compute and compare against, but not to dereference. Both styles, indexing and pointer walking, produce the same machine code in most compilers, so choose whichever is clearer. Index style is usually easier for beginners.

Arrays are not pointers: Despite the close relationship, an array and a pointer are different things. An array is a block of elements; a pointer is a single variable holding an address. sizeof(a) for int a[5] is 20 (the whole array), while sizeof(p) is the size of a pointer, often 8. You can change a pointer, p++ or p = &x, but you cannot change an array name: a++ and a = p are errors, because a is not a variable that stores an address; it is the array itself. Exams like the question "difference between an array and a pointer" precisely because of these points.

Passing arrays to functions, explained: When you pass an array to a function, C passes the address of its first element. So in the function header, int a[] and int *a mean exactly the same thing: void printAll(int a[], int n) and void printAll(int *a, int n) are identical. This explains two facts from lesson 15: the function can change the caller's array, because it works through the address; and sizeof inside the function gives the pointer size, so the length must be passed separately.

The problem with call by value: In lesson 12, void addTen(int x) { x += 10; } could not change the caller's variable, because x was a copy. The classic example is swapping: void swap(int a, int b) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; } swaps only the copies. After swap(x, y); in main, x and y are unchanged. The fix is to give the function the addresses of x and y, so it can reach the originals.

Call by reference with pointers: void swap(int *a, int *b) { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; } and call it as swap(&x, &y);. Now a holds the address of x and b holds the address of y. *a is x itself, so *a = *b copies y into x, and *b = t puts the old x into y. If x was 3 and y was 7, after the call x is 7 and y is 3. Strictly speaking, C still passes the pointers by value (the addresses are copied), but because the copies point to the originals, the effect is called call by reference, or pass by address.

Why scanf needs &: Now the mystery of lesson 5 is solved. scanf must store a value into your variable, so it needs the variable's address: scanf("%d", &x);. Without &, scanf receives the value of x (some garbage number), treats it as an address, and writes somewhere random, which is why forgetting & often crashes. For a char array, the name already is an address, so no & is needed.

Returning more than one value: A function can return only one value with return, but it can give back more results through pointer parameters. void minMax(int a[], int n, int *min, int *max) { *min = *max = a[0]; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) { if (a[i] < *min) *min = a[i]; if (a[i] > *max) *max = a[i]; } }. Call it as minMax(marks, 5, &lo, &hi);, and both lo and hi are filled in. Many standard functions work this way; for example, the return value reports success or failure, while the real results come back through pointer parameters.

Example: dividing with quotient and remainder: void divide(int a, int b, int *q, int *r) { *q = a / b; *r = a % b; }. Calling divide(17, 5, &q, &r); sets q to 3 and r to 2. This pattern, inputs as normal parameters and outputs as pointer parameters, is very common in C. It is good style to name output parameters clearly, like outQuotient, so readers know they will be changed.

Never return the address of a local variable: A function's local variables die when it returns, as you learned in lesson 13. So int *bad(void) { int x = 5; return &x; } returns the address of memory that no longer belongs to x. Using that pointer later is undefined behavior; it may seem to work, then break mysteriously. If a function must create something that outlives the call, use static variables, memory from malloc (next lesson), or let the caller pass in a place to store the result.

Pointers to pointers in functions: If a function must change a pointer variable itself, not just the data it points to, you pass the address of that pointer, which is a pointer to a pointer. void setToNull(int **pp) { *pp = NULL; } called as setToNull(&p); makes p NULL in the caller. You will use this when a function allocates memory and must hand the new address back through a parameter. It is just one more level of the same idea: to change something in the caller, pass its address.

const with pointers: The keyword const can protect data from accidental changes, and with pointers it has two positions. const int *p (or int const *p) means p points to a constant int: you can move p, but you cannot change *p. int *const p means p itself is constant: it always points to the same place, but you may change *p. const int *const p protects both. Read declarations from right to left: in int *const p, "p is a const pointer to int".

const in function parameters: Functions that only read an array should declare it as const: double average(const int a[], int n). Now if the function accidentally writes a[i] = 0, the compiler stops you. It also tells readers, "I promise not to change your data". The standard library does this everywhere; strlen is declared as taking const char *, meaning it only reads the string. Using const for read-only parameters is a sign of a careful C programmer.

Pointers and strings: A string literal like "Dhaka" is stored in read-only memory, and char *city = "Dhaka"; makes city point to its first character. You can read and print it, but writing city[0] = 'd'; is undefined behavior and often crashes. If you want a modifiable copy, use an array: char city[] = "Dhaka";, which copies the characters into your own array. Safer still, write const char *city = "Dhaka"; so the compiler catches any attempt to modify it.

Arrays of pointers: char *days[] = {"Saturday", "Sunday", "Monday"}; is an array of three pointers, each pointing to a string literal. Compared with char days[3][10], it uses only as much space as each string needs and makes swapping two names as cheap as swapping two pointers. Sorting an array of pointers to strings, by swapping pointers instead of copying characters, is a classic efficient technique. The main function can also receive such an array, char *argv[], holding command-line arguments, which you will meet in lesson 24.

Real life example 1, a bank transfer function: Imagine void transfer(double *from, double *to, double amount) { if (*from >= amount) { *from -= amount; *to += amount; } } called as transfer(&rahimBalance, &karimBalance, 500);. Because the function receives addresses, it changes the real balances. With call by value, it would move money between copies and the real balances would stay the same, a very expensive bug. Every banking system relies on functions that modify shared records through references like this.

Real life example 2, a game character update: In a game, void applyDamage(int *health, int damage) { *health -= damage; if (*health < 0) *health = 0; } is called as applyDamage(&player.health, 30);. One small function updates whatever health value you point it to: the player's, an enemy's or a boss's. Passing a pointer lets one function work on many different variables, which keeps game code short and consistent.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: writing swap with plain ints and wondering why nothing changes, calling swap(x, y) instead of swap(&x, &y), using sizeof on an array parameter, trying a++ on an array name, returning the address of a local variable, modifying a string literal, and mixing up const int *p with int *const p. Exams ask: explain the relation between arrays and pointers; why a[i] equals *(a + i); differentiate call by value and call by reference with the swap example; why scanf needs &; how to return multiple values from a function; difference between an array and a pointer; and the meaning of const pointer declarations.

Recap: An array name acts as a pointer to its first element, and a[i] is *(a + i). Arrays and pointers are still different: sizeof differs and an array name cannot be reassigned. Passing an array passes an address, so functions can change it. Passing &x lets a function change x: that is call by reference, the swap function and the reason scanf needs &. Pointer parameters return extra results; never return the address of a local. const protects pointed-to data or the pointer itself. Next: getting memory at runtime with malloc and free.
key_points: An array name converts to a pointer to its first element: a means &a[0].
a[i] is defined as *(a + i); p[i] works the same for a pointer p.
Arrays are not pointers: sizeof differs and a++ or a = p are errors.
int a[] and int *a mean the same in a function parameter list.
Call by reference: pass &x and use *p inside, as in swap(&x, &y).
Pointer parameters let a function return several results.
Never return the address of a local variable.
const int *p protects the data; int *const p protects the pointer.
lessons.tip: Every time a function must change something in the caller, say: 'pass its address, then use star inside'. If you hear yourself say it, you will not forget the & or the *.
lessons.task: Write void swap(int *a, int *b), void minMax(int a[], int n, int *min, int *max) and void divide(int a, int b, int *q, int *r). Test each from main and print the values before and after each call.

quiz.q: For int a[5], what is a[3] equivalent to?
quiz.explain: C defines a[i] as *(a + i).

quiz.q: Why does void swap(int a, int b) fail to swap the caller's variables?
options: It receives copies, not the originals
quiz.explain: Call by value gives the function copies; changing them does not affect the caller.

quiz.q: How should swap(int *a, int *b) be called for x and y?
quiz.explain: The function needs the addresses of x and y.

quiz.q: Which is NOT allowed for int a[5]; int *p = a;?
quiz.explain: An array name cannot be changed; a++ is an error.

quiz.q: What does const int *p mean?
options: The int pointed to cannot be changed through p
quiz.explain: const before the type protects the pointed-to value; the pointer itself can move.

lessons.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation
lessons.content:
Imagine organising a picnic. If you book a bus for exactly 40 seats a month in advance, you are stuck when 55 friends want to come, or you waste money when only 20 show up. It would be much better to decide the size on the day, when you know how many people are coming, and return the bus afterwards. Arrays with a fixed size are like that pre-booked bus: the size is decided when you write the program.
