Dynamic memory allocation lets your program ask for exactly as much memory as it needs while it is running, and give it back when done. In C, this is done with malloc, calloc, realloc and free.

Why fixed arrays are not enough: int marks[100]; reserves space for 100 students whether you have 5 or 5,000. If you have 5, you waste memory; if you have 5,000, the program breaks or overflows. Also, local arrays live on the stack, which is limited in size (often a few megabytes), so a huge local array like int big[10000000]; can crash the program. And local variables die when the function returns, so a function cannot create a list and hand it back safely. Dynamic memory solves all three problems.

Stack and heap: As mentioned in lesson 13, a running program's memory includes the stack and the heap. The stack holds function calls and their local variables; it is managed automatically, fast, and limited. The heap is a large pool of memory that the program manages by hand: you request blocks from it at runtime, and they stay allocated until you release them, regardless of which function is running. Heap memory is accessed only through pointers, because it has no variable name.

The functions and their header: The dynamic memory functions are declared in stdlib.h. malloc allocates a block. calloc allocates and fills it with zeros. realloc resizes a block. free releases a block back to the heap. All the allocation functions return a void * pointer to the block, or NULL if the request cannot be satisfied, so you must always check the result.

malloc: malloc(size) allocates size bytes and returns a pointer to the first byte. To get space for n integers: int *a = malloc(n * sizeof(int));. The sizeof makes the code correct on any machine. An even safer idiom is int *a = malloc(n * sizeof *a);, which stays correct even if you later change the type of a. The memory from malloc is not initialized; it contains garbage, just like an uninitialized local variable. In C, you do not need to cast the result of malloc, because void * converts automatically to any object pointer type; C++ is different, which is why some books write (int *)malloc(...).

Always check for NULL: If there is not enough memory, malloc returns NULL. Using that NULL pointer would crash. So the standard pattern is: int *a = malloc(n * sizeof *a); if (a == NULL) { printf("Out of memory\n"); return 1; }. On a desktop with gigabytes of RAM, small requests rarely fail, but programs on small devices, or programs asking for huge blocks, do hit this case, and professional code always checks.

Using the block like an array: Once you have the pointer, you use it exactly like an array, thanks to lesson 20: a[i] means *(a + i). for (i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%d", &a[i]); reads n values, and all your array algorithms, sum, max, sorting, searching, work unchanged. The only difference is that sizeof(a) gives the pointer size, not the block size, so you must keep track of n yourself.

calloc: calloc(count, size) allocates memory for count elements of size bytes each and sets every byte to zero. int *a = calloc(n, sizeof *a); gives n integers all equal to 0. It is handy for counters and frequency arrays, where you need a clean start. Apart from the zeroing and the two-argument form, it behaves like malloc, including returning NULL on failure.

realloc: realloc(ptr, newSize) changes the size of a previously allocated block. It may grow or shrink the block in place, or allocate a new block, copy the old contents, free the old block, and return the new address. So always use the returned pointer. But careful: if realloc fails, it returns NULL and the old block is still allocated. Writing a = realloc(a, newSize); would then lose the only pointer to the old block. The safe pattern is: int *tmp = realloc(a, newSize); if (tmp == NULL) { handle the error; } else { a = tmp; }.

A growing list with realloc: A common technique is to start small and double the capacity when the array fills up. Start with capacity 4. When the fifth item arrives, realloc to 8; at the ninth, realloc to 16; and so on. Doubling means the total copying work stays small on average. This is exactly how dynamic arrays in many languages, such as vectors in C++ and lists in Python, grow behind the scenes, and you will analyse it properly in the data structures course.

free: free(ptr) gives a block back to the heap so it can be reused. Every block you get from malloc, calloc or realloc should be freed exactly once when you no longer need it. free(NULL) is allowed and does nothing, which makes cleanup code simpler. You must pass free the exact pointer that the allocation returned, not a pointer into the middle of the block, and never pass it the address of a normal variable or array.

Memory leaks: If you lose the last pointer to a block without freeing it, the block stays reserved but nobody can use or free it. This is a memory leak. Example: void f(void) { int *p = malloc(100 * sizeof *p); } leaks 400 bytes every time f is called, because p disappears at the end of f. A small leak in a short program does little harm, because the operating system reclaims all memory when the program exits. But in a server or a phone app that runs for days, leaks slowly eat memory until the program or device slows down or crashes.

Dangling pointers and double free: After free(p), the pointer p still holds the old address, but the memory no longer belongs to you. p is now a dangling pointer. Using *p after free is undefined behavior: it may print old data, garbage, or crash later in a totally different place, which makes these bugs very hard to find. Calling free(p) twice is called a double free and is also undefined behavior. A simple defence is to set p = NULL; right after free(p);, so accidental use crashes quickly and a second free(p) becomes harmless.

A complete example: Read n, then n marks, and print the average. int n; scanf("%d", &n); int *m = malloc(n * sizeof *m); if (m == NULL) return 1; int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { scanf("%d", &m[i]); sum += m[i]; } printf("%.2f\n", (double)sum / n); free(m); m = NULL;. The array is exactly the size the user needs, whether 3 or 30,000, and it is returned when done. This small pattern, allocate, check, use, free, is the core of dynamic memory in C.

Returning dynamic memory from functions: Unlike a local array, heap memory survives after the function returns, so a function can safely create and return it. int *makeArray(int n) { int *a = calloc(n, sizeof *a); return a; } is fine, as long as the caller checks for NULL and later frees the memory. A good habit is to document who is responsible for freeing: "the caller must free the returned array". Ownership confusion, where nobody frees or two places free, is the root of most leaks and double frees.

Dynamic strings: Strings can be allocated too. To copy a name of unknown length: char *copy = malloc(strlen(name) + 1); if (copy != NULL) strcpy(copy, name);. The + 1 is for the '\0', and forgetting it is a classic off-by-one bug that writes one byte past the block. Programs that build text, like report generators or chat apps, allocate and grow strings this way.

Dynamic 2D arrays: For a table whose size is known only at runtime, one approach is an array of row pointers: int **t = malloc(rows * sizeof *t); then for each row, t[i] = malloc(cols * sizeof *t[i]);. You can then write t[i][j] as usual. Freeing is done in reverse: free each row, then free t. Another approach is one big block of rows × cols ints with the index i * cols + j, the same row-major formula from lesson 17, which needs only one malloc and one free.

Tools that help: Memory bugs are hard to see, so programmers use tools. On Linux, Valgrind can report leaks and invalid reads or writes, and compilers such as gcc and clang offer AddressSanitizer with the -fsanitize=address option, which stops the program at the first bad memory access and prints where it happened. Learning to use one of these early will save you many hours in data structures labs.

Real life example 1, a contacts app: When you open your phone's contacts, the app does not know in advance whether you have 50 or 5,000 contacts. It allocates memory as it loads them, growing the list when needed, and frees screens and images you are no longer looking at. If it leaked memory every time you scrolled, the app would get slower and slower until the phone closed it. Careful allocation and freeing is what keeps apps smooth.

Real life example 2, a ticket booking server: A ticket booking system for Eid bus tickets faces a huge rush for a few hours. Each booking request needs some memory for its data, allocated when the request arrives and freed when it finishes. A tiny leak per request, multiplied by hundreds of thousands of requests, could exhaust the server's memory exactly when it is busiest. Real servers are tested specifically for leaks before such high-traffic days.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: not checking for NULL, forgetting sizeof (malloc(n) instead of malloc(n * sizeof(int))), using malloc'd memory as if it were zeroed, a = realloc(a, ...) losing the old block on failure, forgetting free (leaks), using memory after free (dangling pointers), freeing twice, and forgetting + 1 for strings. Exams ask: what is dynamic memory allocation and why use it; difference between stack and heap; difference between malloc and calloc; explain realloc and free; what are memory leaks and dangling pointers; and write a program that allocates an array of n elements at runtime, uses it, and frees it.

Recap: Dynamic allocation lets a program request heap memory at runtime. malloc gives uninitialized memory, calloc gives zeroed memory, realloc resizes (use a temporary pointer), and free returns memory. Always check for NULL, use sizeof, and free each block exactly once. Lost pointers cause leaks, and using freed memory causes dangling-pointer bugs; setting pointers to NULL after free helps. Next we group related data together with structures and unions.
key_points: Dynamic memory comes from the heap at runtime; functions are in stdlib.h.
malloc(n * sizeof *p) returns uninitialized memory or NULL on failure.
calloc(count, size) returns zero-filled memory.
realloc may move the block; assign its result to a temporary pointer first.
free each allocated block exactly once; free(NULL) is safe.
A memory leak is allocated memory with no pointer left to free it.
Using memory after free (dangling pointer) or freeing twice is undefined behavior; set p = NULL after free.
Heap memory survives function returns, so functions may return it; the caller must free it.
lessons.tip: Write every malloc together with its free at the same time, even before writing the code in between. Then fill in the middle. You will almost never leak memory.
lessons.task: Write a program that reads n, allocates an array of n doubles with malloc, reads n prices, prints the total and the most expensive, then frees the memory. Then rewrite it so the array starts with capacity 2 and doubles with realloc while reading until the user enters 0.

quiz.q: Which function returns zero-initialized memory?
quiz.explain: calloc sets all allocated bytes to zero.

quiz.q: What does malloc return when it cannot allocate memory?
quiz.explain: malloc returns NULL on failure, so the result must be checked.

quiz.q: What is a memory leak?
options: Allocated memory that is never freed and no longer reachable
quiz.explain: Losing the last pointer to a block without freeing it leaks that memory.

quiz.q: Why is a = realloc(a, newSize); risky?
options: If realloc fails it returns NULL and the old block is lost
quiz.explain: On failure the old block stays allocated but the only pointer to it is overwritten with NULL.

quiz.q: How much memory should you allocate to copy a string s?
quiz.explain: One extra byte is needed for the terminating '\0'.

lessons.title: Structures, Unions and Enums
lessons.content:
Look at your student ID card. It has your name, your roll number, your department, your blood group and maybe your CGPA. These pieces are different types: text, numbers, a decimal. Yet they all belong together, because they describe one student. Keeping them in five separate arrays, names[], rolls[], depts[], bloods[] and cgpas[], works, but it is clumsy and easy to mix up. C lets you bundle related pieces into one new type called a structure. In this lesson you will learn structures, how to access their members, arrays of structures, structures with pointers and functions, typedef, and two relatives: unions and enums.

What a structure is: A structure, declared with the keyword struct, is a user-defined type that groups variables of possibly different types under one name. Each variable inside is called a member or field. struct Student { int roll; char name[30]; float cgpa; }; defines a new type, struct Student, with three members. Note the semicolon after the closing brace; forgetting it gives confusing errors. Defining the struct only describes the shape, like a blank form; no memory is used until you create variables of that type.

Declaring structure variables: Once the type exists, declare variables like any other type: struct Student s1, s2;. Each variable has its own copy of all members. You can also declare variables right after the definition: struct Student { ... } s1, s2;. Most programs define the struct type at the top of the file, outside functions, so that every function can use it.

Initializing: You can initialize a structure with values in member order: struct Student s1 = {101, "Nusrat Jahan", 3.85};. Since C99 you can also use designated initializers, naming the members: struct Student s2 = {.roll = 102, .cgpa = 3.60, .name = "Tanvir"};, in any order. Members you leave out are set to zero, just like arrays.

Accessing members with the dot: Use the dot operator to reach a member: s1.roll, s1.name, s1.cgpa. Each behaves like an ordinary variable of its type. s1.cgpa = 3.90; changes the CGPA, printf("%s\n", s1.name); prints the name, and scanf("%d", &s1.roll); reads a roll number (the & applies to the member). To set the name later, use strcpy(s1.name, "Nusrat");, because name is a char array and arrays cannot be assigned with =.

Assigning and comparing structures: Unlike arrays, whole structures can be assigned: s2 = s1; copies every member, including arrays inside the structure. That is a convenient surprise. But you cannot compare structures with ==; s1 == s2 is a compile error. To check equality, compare the members you care about, for example s1.roll == s2.roll.

Memory layout and sizeof: A structure's members are stored in order in one block of memory. But sizeof(struct Student) is not always the plain sum of the member sizes, because the compiler may add unused padding bytes so that each member sits at an address that suits the hardware. For example, struct { char c; int x; } is usually 8 bytes, not 5, because 3 padding bytes follow c so that x starts at a multiple of 4. Always use sizeof instead of adding sizes by hand.

Nested structures: A structure can contain another structure. struct Date { int day, month, year; }; struct Student { int roll; char name[30]; struct Date birth; };. Access goes one dot per level: s1.birth.year = 2006;. Nesting keeps related data organised, like an address made of house, road, area and district.

Arrays of structures: Real programs handle many records, so arrays of structures are everywhere: struct Student cls[60];. cls[i] is one student, and cls[i].cgpa is that student's CGPA. Reading all of them: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%d %29s %f", &cls[i].roll, cls[i].name, &cls[i].cgpa);. Finding the topper is the max search from lesson 15, comparing cls[i].cgpa and remembering the index. Sorting by CGPA uses the bubble or selection sort from lesson 16, comparing CGPAs and swapping whole structures with a temporary struct Student variable, which works because structures can be assigned.

Pointers to structures and the arrow: You can point to a structure: struct Student *p = &s1;. To reach a member through the pointer you could write (*p).cgpa; the brackets are needed because . binds tighter than *. Since this is so common, C has the arrow operator: p->cgpa means exactly (*p).cgpa. So p->roll = 105; changes s1.roll. Use the dot with a structure variable and the arrow with a pointer to a structure.

Structures and functions: You can pass a structure to a function by value: void print(struct Student s). The function gets a copy of the whole structure, so changes do not affect the caller, and copying a big structure costs time and memory. Passing a pointer is usually better: void raiseCgpa(struct Student *s, float bonus) { s->cgpa += bonus; }, called as raiseCgpa(&s1, 0.1);. For read-only functions, use const struct Student *s, which is efficient and safe. Functions can also return a structure, which is a neat way to return several values together: struct Date today(void) { struct Date d = {3, 10, 2026}; return d; }.

typedef: Writing struct Student everywhere gets long. typedef creates a new name, an alias, for an existing type: typedef struct Student Student; or in one go, typedef struct { int roll; char name[30]; float cgpa; } Student;. Now you can declare Student s1; without the word struct. typedef works for any type: typedef unsigned long long ull; lets you write ull big = 1;. It does not create a really new type, only a shorter or clearer name.

Self-referential structures, a preview: A structure cannot contain itself, but it can contain a pointer to its own type: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };. Each node holds a value and the address of the next node, forming a chain called a linked list. Together with malloc from lesson 21, this is the foundation of the data structures course: linked lists, stacks, queues and trees are all built from such structures.

Structures with dynamic memory: Structures and malloc work well together. Student *list = malloc(n * sizeof *list); creates room for exactly n students at runtime, and list[i].cgpa or (list + i)->cgpa reaches each one. A single structure can also be allocated: Student *s = malloc(sizeof *s); if (s != NULL) { s->roll = 7; }. As always, check for NULL and free the memory when done. This combination, records allocated on demand and linked by pointers, is how real programs keep collections whose size changes, like the cart in a shopping app.

Unions: A union looks like a structure, but all its members share the same memory. union Value { int i; float f; char c; };. The size of the union is at least the size of its largest member (plus any padding), and only one member holds a meaningful value at a time. If you store v.i = 65; and then read v.f, you get the same bits interpreted as a float, which is generally not meaningful. Unions save memory when a variable can be one of several types but never more than one at once.

Union in practice: Unions are often paired with a tag that says which member is currently valid: struct Item { int type; union { int count; double weight; } amount; };. If type is 0, the item is sold by count; if 1, by weight. Code checks type before reading the right member. Embedded and systems programmers also use unions to view the same bytes in different ways, for example to inspect the bytes of a value, but that touches on implementation details beyond this course.

Structure versus union: In a structure, every member has its own memory, so size is at least the sum of members, and all members can hold values at the same time. In a union, members overlap, so size is that of the largest member, and only one member is valid at a time. For struct { int i; double d; } on a typical system, sizeof is 16 (4 + 4 padding + 8). For union { int i; double d; }, sizeof is 8. This comparison is a very common exam question.

Enumerations: An enum gives names to a set of integer constants. enum Day { SAT, SUN, MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI };. By default, the first name is 0 and each next one is 1 more, so SAT is 0 and FRI is 6. You can set values: enum Grade { F = 0, D = 1, C = 2, B = 3, A = 4 }; or enum Status { OK = 200, NOT_FOUND = 404 };. An enum variable, enum Day today = MON;, is really an integer, but the names make code self-explanatory, especially with switch: case MON: reads far better than case 2:.

Real life example 1, a university result system: A result program might define typedef struct { char code[10]; float credit; float gradePoint; } Course; and typedef struct { int roll; char name[40]; Course courses[8]; int nCourses; float cgpa; } Student;. One Student holds everything about a student, including an array of Course structures. A function float computeCgpa(const Student *s) loops over s->courses, and an array Student batch[120]; holds the whole batch. This is exactly how real records are organised, from schools to banks.

Real life example 2, a food delivery order: An order in a food delivery app could be a structure with an order ID, customer name, restaurant, an array of items (each itself a structure with name, quantity and price), a delivery address (a nested structure) and a status enum: enum Status { PLACED, PREPARING, ON_THE_WAY, DELIVERED };. Updating the status through a pointer, updateStatus(&order, ON_THE_WAY), changes the real order. Structures, nesting, pointers and enums all work together in one small model of a real system.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: forgetting the semicolon after the struct definition, using = to set a char array member instead of strcpy, comparing structures with ==, using . with a pointer or -> with a variable, writing *p.cgpa instead of p->cgpa, assuming sizeof equals the sum of members, and reading a different union member from the one last written. Exams ask: define a structure and how it differs from an array; write a program with an array of structures to store and print student records or find the highest CGPA; explain the arrow operator; difference between structure and union with sizes; what is typedef; and what is an enum with an example.

Recap: A structure groups members of different types into one user-defined type; access members with . for variables and -> for pointers. Structures can be assigned but not compared with ==, nested, put in arrays, and passed to functions, preferably by pointer. typedef gives types shorter names. Self-referential structures with pointers lead to linked lists. A union overlaps its members in one block sized for the largest, and an enum names integer constants. Next: saving data permanently with file handling.
key_points: A struct groups related members of different types into one new type; end its definition with a semicolon.
Access members with . on a variable and -> on a pointer: p->x is (*p).x.
Structures can be assigned with = but not compared with ==.
sizeof a struct may be larger than the sum of its members because of padding.
Arrays of structures hold many records: cls[i].cgpa.
Pass large structures by pointer (const for read-only) instead of by value.
typedef creates an alias: typedef struct {...} Student;
A union's members share memory (size of the largest); an enum names integer constants starting at 0.
lessons.tip: Before coding, design your struct on paper as a form with labelled boxes. If a box would hold several values of the same kind, make it an array; if it is a group of fields, make it a nested struct.
lessons.task: Define typedef struct { int roll; char name[30]; float cgpa; } Student; read 5 students into an array, print them in a table, print the student with the highest CGPA, and sort the array by CGPA in descending order.

quiz.q: If p is a pointer to a structure, how do you access its member cgpa?
quiz.explain: The arrow operator accesses a member through a pointer; it equals (*p).cgpa.

quiz.q: Which operation is NOT allowed on two struct variables s1 and s2 of the same type?
quiz.explain: Structures can be assigned but cannot be compared with ==.

quiz.q: What is the size of a union?
options: At least the size of its largest member
quiz.explain: All members share the same memory, so it must fit the largest one.

quiz.q: In enum Day { SAT, SUN, MON }; what is the value of MON?
quiz.explain: Enum constants start at 0 by default: SAT 0, SUN 1, MON 2.

quiz.q: Why can sizeof(struct { char c; int x; }) be 8 instead of 5?
options: The compiler adds padding for alignment
quiz.explain: Padding bytes are inserted so that x starts at an address suitable for an int.

lessons.title: File Handling
lessons.content:
Write a list of marks on a whiteboard and it is gone the moment someone wipes it. Write the same list in a notebook and you can read it next week, next year, or give it to a friend. So far, every value your programs stored lived in RAM, like the whiteboard: when the program ends, all the data vanishes. To keep data after the program closes, you must write it to a file on the disk, the notebook. File handling lets a C program create files, write to them, read them back, add to them and move around inside them. This is how real programs save settings, records, logs and documents.

Why files: Files give persistence: data survives after the program ends and even after the computer restarts. They also let programs handle more data than you would want to type every time, such as reading 10,000 student records from a file instead of the keyboard. And files let programs share data: one program writes a report, another reads it, or you open it in a text editor. Almost every useful program you will build later, from a library system to a game with save slots, uses files.

Text and binary files: A text file stores data as readable characters, line by line, like a .txt or .csv file; the number 1234 is stored as the four characters '1', '2', '3', '4'. A binary file stores the raw bytes of values exactly as they sit in memory; the int 1234 is stored as its 4-byte binary form. Text files are easy to read and edit by humans and portable between systems. Binary files are compact and fast to read and write, but you cannot read them in a text editor, and their layout can depend on the machine. C handles both with the same set of functions in stdio.h.

The FILE pointer: In C, a file is accessed through a pointer to a structure of type FILE, defined in stdio.h. FILE *fp; declares such a pointer. You never look inside the FILE structure yourself; you just pass fp to the file functions, and the library keeps track of the position in the file, the buffer and errors. In fact, the keyboard and screen are already FILE pointers: stdin, stdout and stderr (for error messages) are opened automatically when your program starts.

Opening a file with fopen: fp = fopen("marks.txt", "r"); opens the file named marks.txt for reading. The first argument is the file name or path, and the second is the mode, a string that says what you want to do. If the file cannot be opened, for example it does not exist or you lack permission, fopen returns NULL. Always check: if (fp == NULL) { printf("Cannot open file\n"); return 1; }. Skipping this check and then reading through a NULL pointer is one of the most common file-handling crashes.

File modes: "r" opens an existing file for reading; it fails if the file does not exist. "w" opens for writing; it creates the file if needed, and if the file exists, it erases its contents first. "a" opens for appending; it creates the file if needed and adds new data at the end without erasing anything. Adding + allows both reading and writing: "r+" reads and writes an existing file, "w+" creates or truncates and then reads and writes, and "a+" reads and appends. Adding b, as in "rb" or "wb", opens in binary mode. Using "w" by mistake on an important file erases it, so choose modes carefully.

Closing with fclose: When you are done, call fclose(fp);. This writes any data still waiting in the buffer to the disk and frees the resources the system uses for the open file. If a program forgets fclose and crashes, the last part of the data may never reach the disk. A program also has a limit on how many files it can have open at once. The rule is like malloc and free: every successful fopen should be matched by exactly one fclose.

Writing formatted text with fprintf: fprintf works exactly like printf, but with a FILE pointer as the first argument: fprintf(fp, "%d %s %.2f\n", roll, name, cgpa);. This writes one line of text to the file. Writing a whole class list is just a loop of fprintf calls. Since stdout is also a FILE pointer, fprintf(stdout, ...) is the same as printf(...), and fprintf(stderr, "Error!\n"); is the standard way to print error messages.

Reading formatted text with fscanf: fscanf is scanf for files: fscanf(fp, "%d %29s %f", &roll, name, &cgpa);. It returns the number of items successfully read, or EOF if the end of the file is reached before anything is read. The standard loop to read all records is while (fscanf(fp, "%d %29s %f", &roll, name, &cgpa) == 3) { process the record }. The loop stops cleanly at the end of the file or at the first badly formatted line.

Character I/O: fgetc and fputc: fgetc(fp) reads one character and returns it as an int, or returns EOF at the end of the file. fputc(c, fp) writes one character. Copying a file character by character: int c; while ((c = fgetc(in)) != EOF) fputc(c, out);. Notice that c is an int, not a char. EOF is a negative value (commonly -1) that must be distinguishable from every real character, and storing the result in a char can break that comparison. This is a classic exam point.

Line I/O: fgets and fputs: fgets(line, sizeof line, fp) reads one line (up to the size limit) including the newline, and returns NULL at the end of the file, so while (fgets(line, sizeof line, fp) != NULL) { ... } reads a file line by line. fputs(line, fp) writes a string without adding a newline. Line-by-line reading is the safest way to process text files, because you can then parse each line with sscanf or string functions.

The feof trap: A very common beginner loop is while (!feof(fp)) { fscanf(...); ... }. It looks natural but is wrong: feof becomes true only after a read has already failed at the end, so the loop body runs one extra time with stale data, often printing the last record twice. The correct approach is to test the return value of the reading function itself, as in the fscanf, fgetc and fgets loops above. Use feof and ferror after the loop if you need to know whether it stopped because of end-of-file or because of an error.

Binary I/O with fwrite and fread: For binary files, fwrite(ptr, size, count, fp) writes count items of size bytes each from memory, and fread(ptr, size, count, fp) reads them back. Both return the number of items actually processed. Saving a whole array of structures is one line: fwrite(students, sizeof(Student), n, fp); and loading is fread(students, sizeof(Student), n, fp);. This is fast and simple, which is why many programs save their data this way, but the file is only reliably readable by a program built with the same structure layout on a similar machine.

Random access: fseek, ftell and rewind: Files are normally read from start to end, but you can jump around. fseek(fp, offset, origin) moves the file position: origin is SEEK_SET (from the start), SEEK_CUR (from the current position) or SEEK_END (from the end). ftell(fp) returns the current position in bytes. rewind(fp) jumps back to the start. With binary records of fixed size, fseek(fp, k * sizeof(Student), SEEK_SET); then fread reaches the k-th record directly, without reading the ones before it. A simple trick to find a file's size: fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END); long size = ftell(fp);.

Other useful functions: remove("old.txt") deletes a file, and rename("a.txt", "b.txt") renames one; both return 0 on success. fflush(fp) forces buffered output to be written now. sprintf and sscanf work like printf and scanf but on strings in memory instead of files, which is handy for building or parsing a line. And since file names are just strings, you can let the user type a file name and open whatever they ask for.

A complete program: Saving and loading marks. Writing: FILE *fp = fopen("marks.txt", "w"); if (fp == NULL) return 1; for (i = 0; i < n; i++) fprintf(fp, "%d %d\n", roll[i], marks[i]); fclose(fp);. Reading back: fp = fopen("marks.txt", "r"); if (fp == NULL) return 1; while (fscanf(fp, "%d %d", &r, &m) == 2) { total += m; count++; } fclose(fp); printf("Average %.2f\n", (double)total / count);. Open, check, loop with a return-value test, close: this skeleton covers most file tasks in a first course.

Real life example 1, a shop's daily sales log: A small shop's billing program appends each sale to sales_2026_10.txt using mode "a": fprintf(fp, "%s %d %.2f\n", item, qty, price);. Nothing old is ever erased, and at the end of the month a separate report program reads the file line by line and totals the sales per item. If the shop's computer restarts, all past sales are still on disk. Append mode for logs is how most real systems record events, from ATMs to web servers.

Real life example 2, a game's save file: A game stores the player's progress in a binary file: a structure with level, score, health and position written with fwrite when the player saves, and read with fread when the game starts. With fixed-size save slots, fseek jumps straight to slot 3 without reading slots 1 and 2. If the game used "w" when it meant "a" or "r+", it could erase all the other slots, which is exactly the kind of bug careful mode choice prevents.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: not checking fopen for NULL, using "w" on a file you wanted to keep, forgetting fclose, using while (!feof(fp)), storing fgetc's result in a char, mixing up the argument order of fprintf (the FILE pointer comes first) or of fread and fwrite, forgetting & in fscanf, and reading a binary file in text mode or the other way round. Exams ask: what is a file and why use files; difference between text and binary files; explain FILE *, fopen and file modes; difference between "w" and "a"; write a program that writes student records to a file and reads them back; copy one file to another; count characters, words or lines in a file; and explain fseek, ftell and rewind.

Recap: Files keep data after a program ends. Access them through a FILE pointer from fopen, always checking for NULL, and close them with fclose. Modes decide what you can do: "r" reads, "w" writes and erases, "a" appends, + adds both, and b means binary. Use fprintf and fscanf for formatted text, fgetc and fputc for characters, fgets and fputs for lines, and fread and fwrite for binary blocks. Control loops with the return values, not feof, and use fseek and ftell to jump. Next: the preprocessor and organising bigger programs into several files.
key_points: Files keep data after the program ends; RAM data is lost.
FILE *fp = fopen(name, mode); always check for NULL, and fclose when done.
"r" read, "w" write (erases existing content), "a" append; + allows read and write; b means binary.
fprintf/fscanf for formatted text; fgetc/fputc for characters; fgets/fputs for lines.
fread/fwrite move raw bytes for binary files, e.g. whole arrays of structures.
Store fgetc's result in an int so it can be compared with EOF.
Loop on the read function's return value, not while (!feof(fp)).
fseek, ftell and rewind give random access within a file.
lessons.tip: Write file code in this exact order: fopen, if NULL then stop, the loop, fclose. Type the fclose line right after the NULL check, then fill in the middle.
lessons.task: Write a program that saves 5 students (roll, name, CGPA) to students.txt with fprintf, then reopens the file, reads them back with a fscanf loop, and prints the average CGPA. Then open the file in a text editor to see what was written.

quiz.q: What happens if you open an existing file with mode "w"?
options: New data is added at the end
quiz.explain: "w" truncates an existing file to zero length before writing.

quiz.q: What does fopen return when it cannot open a file?
quiz.explain: fopen returns a NULL pointer on failure, which must be checked.

quiz.q: Why should the result of fgetc be stored in an int?
options: So it can be compared reliably with EOF
quiz.explain: EOF is a negative int value that must be distinguishable from every character.

quiz.q: Which mode adds data to the end of a file without erasing it?
quiz.explain: Append mode writes at the end and keeps existing content.

quiz.q: Why is while (!feof(fp)) { fscanf(...); } usually wrong?
options: feof only becomes true after a read fails, so the last record is often processed twice
quiz.explain: The loop should test the return value of fscanf instead.

lessons.title: Preprocessor and Program Organisation
lessons.content:
Before a big cricket match, the ground staff prepares everything: they roll the pitch, paint the lines, set up the stumps and the boundary rope. Only then do the players walk out. The C preprocessor is that ground staff. Before the compiler sees a single line of your code, the preprocessor goes through the file, pastes in headers, replaces macros, and decides which parts of the code should even be compiled. In this lesson you will learn the preprocessor directives properly, then use them to split a big program into several files with header files, and finally learn how main can receive arguments from the command line.

What the preprocessor is: The preprocessor is the first stage of building a C program, as you saw in lesson 2. It works on the text of your source file, not on its meaning. Every line that starts with # is a preprocessor directive, an instruction for this stage. Directives do not end with a semicolon. The output of the preprocessor is pure C code with all headers pasted in and all macros replaced, which then goes to the compiler. You can see it yourself with gcc -E file.c.

#include: #include copies the entire contents of another file into this spot. There are two forms. #include <stdio.h> with angle brackets searches the system's standard header directories; use it for library headers. #include "student.h" with double quotes first searches the directory of the current file, then the system directories; use it for your own headers. A header file normally contains declarations, such as prototypes, type definitions and macros, so that many .c files can share them.

#define for constants: #define NAME replacement creates an object-like macro. #define MAX_STUDENTS 120 makes the preprocessor replace every later MAX_STUDENTS token with 120 before compiling. By convention, macro names are in capitals so readers can tell them apart from variables. Macros like this are used for array sizes, limits and fixed settings. Remember from lesson 3: no = sign and no semicolon; #define PI = 3.14; would paste "= 3.14;" everywhere PI appears, causing strange errors.

Function-like macros: A macro can take parameters: #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)). Then SQUARE(5) becomes ((5) * (5)), which is 25. It looks like a function call, but it is pure text replacement done before compiling, with no type checking and no function call overhead. #define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b)) is another classic. Note there must be no space between the macro name and the opening bracket in the definition, otherwise it becomes an object-like macro whose text starts with a bracket.

Why all the brackets: Because macros replace text blindly, missing brackets cause wrong answers. With #define SQUARE(x) x * x, the call SQUARE(2 + 3) becomes 2 + 3 * 2 + 3, which is 11, not 25. With #define DOUBLE(x) (x) + (x), the expression 10 * DOUBLE(3) becomes 10 * (3) + (3), which is 33, not 60. The rule: put brackets around every parameter and around the whole macro body. Exams love asking for the output of a badly bracketed macro.

Side effects in macros: Even with brackets, a macro may evaluate its argument more than once. SQUARE(i++) becomes ((i++) * (i++)), which modifies i twice in one expression, undefined behavior as you learned in lesson 6. A real function int square(int x) evaluates its argument once. This is why modern C prefers real functions, possibly marked inline (a C99 keyword that suggests the compiler insert the body directly), for anything more than trivial macros.

#undef and predefined macros: #undef NAME removes a macro definition, so later lines no longer replace NAME. The compiler also provides predefined macros: __FILE__ is the current file name as a string, __LINE__ the current line number, __DATE__ and __TIME__ the compile date and time. printf("Error in %s at line %d\n", __FILE__, __LINE__); is a handy debugging trick that prints exactly where the message came from.

Conditional compilation: The preprocessor can include or skip parts of the code depending on conditions. #if expression ... #elif ... #else ... #endif works like if-else but at compile time, using constant expressions. #ifdef NAME includes the following code only if NAME is defined as a macro, and #ifndef NAME only if it is not. Example: #define DEBUG then later #ifdef DEBUG printf("x = %d\n", x); #endif. Remove the #define DEBUG line, and every debug print disappears from the compiled program without deleting any code.

Uses of conditional compilation: Programmers use it to write code that compiles on different systems, for example #ifdef _WIN32 for Windows-specific code; to switch features on and off; to keep debug output out of the final version; and, most importantly, for include guards. You can also define macros from the command line: gcc -DDEBUG main.c defines DEBUG without editing the file, a common way to build a debug version.

Include guards: If a header is included twice in the same .c file, perhaps indirectly through another header, its type definitions would appear twice and cause errors. The standard fix is an include guard: at the top of student.h write #ifndef STUDENT_H, then #define STUDENT_H, then the header's contents, and #endif at the very end. The first time, STUDENT_H is not defined, so the contents are included and STUDENT_H gets defined. The second time, #ifndef is false and the whole file is skipped. Every header you write should have one. Many compilers also accept #pragma once for the same purpose, but it is not part of the C standard.

Macro or function, the comparison: A macro is expanded by the preprocessor, has no type checking, may evaluate arguments more than once, and makes the program slightly larger because its text is copied at every use, but it has no call overhead. A function is compiled once, checks argument types, evaluates each argument exactly once, and can be debugged and stepped through, at the small cost of a call. For anything with logic, choose a function; keep macros for constants, simple expressions and conditional compilation. This macro-versus-function table is one of the most frequently asked short questions on this topic.

Splitting a program into files: As programs grow past a few hundred lines, one file becomes hard to manage. The usual structure is: a header file, such as student.h, with the include guard, the struct and typedef definitions, macros and function prototypes; a source file, student.c, that includes student.h and defines those functions; and main.c, which includes student.h and calls the functions. Each .c file is a separate module with a clear job, just as functions are, but at a bigger scale.

What goes where: Put declarations in headers: prototypes, type definitions, macros, and extern declarations of shared global variables. Put definitions in .c files: function bodies and the actual global variables (defined exactly once). Never define a normal function or a global variable in a header, because if two .c files include it, the linker sees two definitions and reports "multiple definition". Helper functions that only one file needs should be declared static in that .c file, as lesson 13 explained, so they stay private.

Compiling several files: You can compile all the files together: gcc main.c student.c -o app. Or compile each into an object file separately and link them: gcc -c main.c, gcc -c student.c, then gcc main.o student.o -o app. Separate compilation means that when you change only student.c, you recompile only that file and relink, which saves a lot of time in big projects. Tools such as make automate this by recompiling only what changed, and IDEs like Code::Blocks do it behind the scenes when you create a project.

Command-line arguments: main can be written to receive what the user typed after the program name: int main(int argc, char *argv[]). argc (argument count) is the number of words, and argv (argument vector) is an array of strings holding them. If you run ./grade 85 Rahim, then argc is 3, argv[0] is "./grade" (the program name), argv[1] is "85" and argv[2] is "Rahim". argv[argc] is guaranteed to be NULL. Many real tools, like gcc itself with its options, are driven entirely by command-line arguments.

Using command-line arguments: Arguments always arrive as strings, so numbers must be converted: int marks = atoi(argv[1]); or, more carefully, with strtol. Always check argc before using argv, otherwise argv[1] may not exist: if (argc < 3) { fprintf(stderr, "Usage: %s marks name\n", argv[0]); return 1; }. A program like ./copy source.txt dest.txt that copies one file to another, combining this lesson with lesson 23, is a classic lab exercise.

Exit codes: The value returned from main, or passed to exit() from stdlib.h, is the program's exit status. By convention 0 means success and non-zero means some kind of failure; stdlib.h also defines EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE. Scripts and other programs check this code to decide what to do next. exit(1); can be called from any function to end the whole program immediately, though returning errors up to main is usually cleaner.

Real life example 1, a library management project: A university library system in C might have book.h and book.c for book records, member.h and member.c for members, storage.c for saving to files, and main.c for the menu. Each header has include guards and prototypes; each .c file is compiled separately. A #define MAX_BOOKS 5000 in a config header controls array sizes everywhere, and #ifdef DEBUG blocks print internal details only in test builds. This is exactly the kind of structure teachers expect in a first-year project.

Real life example 2, a command-line unit converter: A small tool called convert can be run as ./convert 5 km mi. main checks that argc is 4, converts argv[1] with atof, compares argv[2] and argv[3] with strcmp to choose the formula, and prints the result, returning 0 on success or 1 with a usage message if the input is wrong. With conditional compilation, the same source can print extra details when built with -DVERBOSE. Small command-line tools like this are everywhere on Linux servers.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mistakes: a semicolon or = in #define, macros without brackets, macros with side-effect arguments, a space between the macro name and its bracket, missing include guards, defining functions or globals in headers, forgetting to compile all the .c files (giving "undefined reference" linker errors), and using argv[1] without checking argc. Exams ask: what is the preprocessor and list its directives; difference between #include <> and ""; difference between a macro and a function; find the output of a given macro; explain conditional compilation and include guards; and write a program using argc and argv.

Recap: The preprocessor runs before compiling and handles # directives. #include pastes headers, #define creates constants and function-like macros that need careful brackets, and #if, #ifdef and #ifndef control which code is compiled, including include guards. Big programs are split into headers for declarations and .c files for definitions, compiled separately and linked together. main(int argc, char *argv[]) receives command-line arguments as strings, and the return value reports success or failure. In the final lesson we bring everything together with debugging, good style and a mini project.
key_points: The preprocessor processes # directives before compiling; directives have no semicolon.
#include <file> searches system headers; #include "file" searches your folder first.
#define creates macros by text replacement; bracket every parameter and the whole body.
Macros can evaluate arguments twice: SQUARE(i++) is undefined behavior; prefer functions.
#if, #ifdef, #ifndef, #else, #endif control what gets compiled.
Include guards (#ifndef X_H / #define X_H / #endif) stop double inclusion.
Headers hold declarations; .c files hold definitions; compile with gcc main.c other.c -o app.
int main(int argc, char *argv[]): argv[0] is the program name; arguments are strings.
lessons.tip: When a macro gives a strange answer, write out its expansion by hand on paper, exactly as the preprocessor would. The bug usually becomes obvious within seconds.
lessons.task: Split a small student program into student.h (include guard, typedef, prototypes), student.c (function bodies) and main.c (menu). Compile with gcc main.c student.c -o app. Then add a program that prints all its command-line arguments with argc and argv.

quiz.q: With #define SQUARE(x) x * x, what is SQUARE(2 + 3)?
quiz.explain: It expands to 2 + 3 * 2 + 3 = 11, which is why parameters need brackets.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an include guard?
options: To prevent a header's contents from being included twice
To hide functions from other files
quiz.explain: #ifndef/#define/#endif skips the header body after its first inclusion.

quiz.q: If you run ./prog hello 42, what is argc?
quiz.explain: The program name, hello and 42 make three arguments.

quiz.q: Which directive includes code only when a macro is NOT defined?
quiz.explain: #ifndef means 'if not defined'.

quiz.q: Why should a normal function not be defined in a header file?
options: If two .c files include it, the linker sees two definitions
quiz.explain: Each including file would define it, causing a multiple-definition linker error.

lessons.title: Debugging, Good Style and a Mini Project
lessons.content:
A mechanic who knows every part of an engine is useful, but the mechanic who can find out why a car is making a strange noise is the one everyone calls. Programming is the same. You have now learned the parts of C: types, operators, decisions, loops, functions, arrays, strings, pointers, structures and files. This final lesson is about the skills that turn knowledge into working programs: finding and fixing bugs, testing, and writing code that other people (and future you) can read. Then we put the whole course together in one mini project, a student result manager, exactly the kind of project many first-year courses ask for.

The debugging mindset: A bug is the difference between what you expected and what the program actually does. Debugging is not guessing and randomly changing lines until the output looks right; that often hides one bug and creates two more. It is a calm, scientific process: reproduce the problem, form a guess about the cause, test the guess, fix the cause, and confirm the fix. Experienced programmers spend a large part of their time debugging, and the good ones are not the ones who never make mistakes, but the ones who find them quickly.

Step one, reproduce: First find an input that always shows the bug. "Sometimes it prints a wrong average" is hard to work with; "with marks 70, 80 and 95 it prints 81 instead of 81.67" is easy. Write the input down. If the bug depends on file contents, keep a small test file. The smaller the input that still shows the bug, the easier the hunt: if it fails for 100 students, try 3; if it still fails, you now have a tiny case to trace by hand.

Reading compiler messages: Many bugs are caught before the program even runs. Read the first error message carefully: it gives the file, the line number and a description, like "expected ';' before 'return'". The real mistake is often on the line before the one reported, such as a missing semicolon. Fix the first error, then compile again, because later errors are often side effects of the first. Turn on warnings with -Wall -Wextra and treat them seriously: warnings about unused variables, implicit declarations, format mismatches or "suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value" point straight at real bugs.

printf debugging: The simplest runtime technique is to print values at key points: printf("DEBUG: i=%d sum=%d\n", i, sum);. Print before and after a suspicious line, inside loops, and at the start of functions with their parameters. Compare what you see with what you expected; the first place where they differ is where the bug lives. Use fprintf(stderr, ...) for debug messages so they are not mixed with normal output, and wrap them in #ifdef DEBUG from lesson 24 so they can be switched off.

Tracing by hand: For small programs, a trace table on paper is powerful. Make a column for each variable and a row for each step, and write the values as you execute the code in your head, exactly as you did for loops, recursion and pointers in earlier lessons. Many students skip this because it feels slow, but it is often faster than staring at the screen, and it is exactly the skill exams test when they ask "what is the output?".

Rubber duck debugging: Programmers have a famous trick: explain your code, line by line, out loud, to a rubber duck, a friend or even an empty chair. While explaining what each line is supposed to do, you often notice that one line does not do what you just said. It sounds silly, but it works because it forces you to slow down and check your assumptions instead of reading what you think you wrote.

Using a debugger: A debugger lets you pause a running program and look inside. On Linux, gdb is the classic: compile with gcc -g prog.c -o prog to include debugging information, then run gdb ./prog. Useful commands: break main sets a breakpoint, run starts the program, next runs one line (stepping over function calls), step runs one line and steps into calls, print sum shows a variable, and backtrace shows the chain of function calls after a crash, which immediately tells you where a segmentation fault happened. IDEs like Code::Blocks and VS Code give the same features with buttons and a variables window.

Assertions: The header assert.h provides assert(condition). If the condition is false at runtime, the program stops and prints the file, line and the failed condition. assert(n > 0); at the start of a function documents and checks an assumption. assert(index >= 0 && index < size); before an array access catches out-of-bounds bugs early. Assertions are for catching programmer mistakes during development, not for handling bad user input; compiling with -DNDEBUG removes them from the final build.

The usual suspects: Most C bugs fall into a few families you have already met. Missing or extra semicolons (lessons 2, 8, 10). = instead of == (lesson 8). Integer division when a decimal was wanted (lesson 6). Uninitialized variables and garbage values (lesson 3). Off-by-one loops and out-of-bounds arrays (lessons 10 and 15). Missing break in switch (lesson 9). Wrong scanf specifiers or a missing & (lesson 5). Missing '\0' or buffer overflows in strings (lesson 18). Wild, NULL or dangling pointers (lessons 19 and 21). Memory leaks (lesson 21). Not checking fopen or using feof wrongly (lesson 23). Unbracketed macros (lesson 24). When stuck, walk through this list.

Testing: Testing means running your program on chosen inputs and checking the outputs against answers you worked out independently. Do not just test the "normal" case. Test boundaries (0, 1, the largest allowed value, exactly the pass mark), empty input (zero students), invalid input (letters where numbers are expected, negative marks), and special cases (all values equal, already sorted data). A small table, input, expected output, actual output, makes testing systematic. Every time you fix a bug, add the input that exposed it to your test list, so it never returns unnoticed.

Testing functions separately: Because you wrote your program as small functions, you can test each one alone. Write a tiny main that calls isLeapYear(1900), isLeapYear(2000) and isLeapYear(2024) and prints the results, or uses assert to check them. When each piece is known to work, bugs in the whole program are much easier to locate. This idea, called unit testing, is used in every professional software team, with frameworks that run thousands of such checks automatically.

Good style, naming and layout: Readable code has fewer bugs and is easier to fix. Use meaningful names: totalMarks, not tm; isValid, not flag2. Indent consistently, usually four spaces per level, and put braces in one consistent style. Keep lines reasonably short and put one statement per line. Leave blank lines between logical sections. Most editors can format C code automatically, and tools like clang-format apply a style for you.

Good style, structure: Keep functions short and focused on one job; if a function is longer than a screen, consider splitting it. Avoid magic numbers: write #define PASS_MARK 40 or const int PASS_MARK = 40; instead of scattering 40 everywhere. Avoid global variables except for a few constants. Use const for parameters you do not change. Check every return value that can signal failure: scanf, malloc, fopen. Comment why, not what: "use 3.0 so the average keeps decimals" is useful, while "add a and b" is noise.

The mini project, design: Let us design a student result manager. Data: typedef struct { int roll; char name[40]; int marks[3]; int total; double avg; char grade; } Student; and an array Student list[MAX]; with a count n. Functions: void addStudent(Student list[], int *n), void computeResult(Student *s), void printAll(const Student list[], int n), int findByRoll(const Student list[], int n, int roll), void sortByTotal(Student list[], int n), int saveToFile(const Student list[], int n, const char *fname) and int loadFromFile(Student list[], int *n, const char *fname). main shows a menu in a do-while loop with a switch: 1 add, 2 show all, 3 search, 4 sort, 5 save, 6 load, 0 exit.

The mini project, how the pieces connect: addStudent reads one record with scanf and fgets, then calls computeResult, which sums the marks with a loop, computes avg = total / 3.0 and assigns the grade with an else-if ladder (lessons 8 and 10). n is passed as a pointer so addStudent can increase it (lesson 20). printAll prints a neat table with %-20s and %6.2f (lesson 5). findByRoll is a linear search returning an index or -1 (lesson 16). sortByTotal is a selection sort swapping whole structures (lessons 16 and 22). saveToFile uses fopen with "w" and fprintf in a loop, and loadFromFile uses an fscanf loop that stops on the return value (lesson 23). Each function is short, testable, and uses one or two ideas from this course.

The mini project, building and testing it: Build it in small steps, compiling and running after each: first the struct and addStudent with printAll, then computeResult, then search, sort, and finally the file functions. Test each step with three students whose results you calculated by hand, including one exactly on a grade boundary and one with all zeros. Try searching for a roll that does not exist, loading a file that does not exist, and adding more students than MAX to see that your checks work. Optional extensions: allocate the array with malloc and grow it with realloc (lesson 21), split the code into student.h, student.c and main.c (lesson 24), or add a command-line argument for the data file name.

Real life example, how teams work: In a software company in Dhaka, a bug report arrives: "The invoice total is wrong for some customers." A developer reproduces it with one customer's data, finds that a discount is calculated with integer division, writes a test with that exact case, fixes the line with a cast, runs all the existing tests to make sure nothing else broke, and gets a teammate to review the change. Reproduce, locate, fix, test, review: the same steps you practised in this lesson, just with more people and more code.

Where to go next: Structured Programming in C is the foundation for nearly everything that follows. Data Structures will use your structs, pointers and malloc to build linked lists, stacks, queues, trees and graphs. Algorithms will analyse the searching and sorting you wrote and give you much faster ones. Object Oriented Programming in C++ or Java builds on the same syntax and adds classes. Operating Systems, Computer Architecture and Networking courses use C to show how machines really work. Keep practising: online judges such as Codeforces, AtCoder, UVa or Toph (a Bangladeshi platform) offer thousands of problems where you can solve, submit and get instant feedback.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Common mistakes at this stage are changing code randomly instead of tracing, ignoring warnings, testing only easy inputs, writing one giant main instead of functions, and not checking return values. Exams and vivas ask: what is debugging and what are common debugging techniques; types of errors with examples; what is a test case and why test boundary values; what makes code readable; and, very often, write a menu-driven program using structures, arrays, functions and files, like the mini project.

Recap: Debugging is a calm cycle of reproduce, locate, fix and confirm, using compiler messages, warnings, printf, hand traces, a rubber duck, a debugger like gdb, and assert. Test normal, boundary, empty and invalid inputs, and test functions one by one. Write readable code with good names, consistent layout, short functions, named constants and checked return values. The mini project shows how every topic of this course fits into one real program. Congratulations: you have finished Structured Programming in C, and you are ready for data structures.
key_points: Debugging is a cycle: reproduce, locate, fix, confirm; never change code randomly.
Fix the first compiler error first; compile with -Wall -Wextra and take warnings seriously.
printf debugging, hand trace tables and explaining code aloud find many bugs.
gcc -g and gdb (break, run, next, step, print, backtrace) let you pause and inspect a program.
assert(condition) from assert.h checks programmer assumptions during development.
Test normal, boundary, empty and invalid inputs, and test each function separately.
Good style: meaningful names, consistent indentation, short functions, named constants, checked return values.
A menu-driven project combines structs, arrays, functions, pointers, sorting, searching and files.
lessons.tip: Keep a 'bug diary': for every bug you fix, write one line with the symptom and the real cause. After a month you will recognise most bugs from their symptoms alone.
lessons.task: Build the student result manager from this lesson step by step: struct and add/print first, then grading, search, sort, and file save/load. Write a test table with at least 6 inputs, including a grade boundary and a roll number that does not exist.

quiz.q: What is the best first step when a program gives a wrong answer?
options: Find an input that reliably reproduces the bug
Change random lines until it works
quiz.explain: A reproducible case lets you trace and test the cause systematically.

quiz.q: Which gdb command shows the chain of function calls after a crash?
quiz.explain: backtrace (bt) lists the active function calls, showing where the crash happened.

quiz.q: What does assert(n > 0); do if n is 0?
options: Stops the program and reports the failed condition
quiz.explain: A failed assertion aborts the program with the file, line and condition.

quiz.q: Which is a boundary test for a pass mark of 40?
quiz.explain: Boundary tests check values exactly at the edge, like 40 and 39.

quiz.q: Why replace 40 with #define PASS_MARK 40?
options: It avoids a magic number and allows one-place changes
quiz.explain: Named constants explain meaning and let you change the value in one place.
